speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At the conclusion of his
long address yesterday, my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said that he would like very much to offer to this side of the house his helpful cooperation in the difficult task with which governments of the present day are confronted. I think it was a fortunate thing for my right hon. friend that he made that statement at the end of his speech rather than at the beginning, because until the moment he made it there had been, I must say, nothing in his remarks which could have been construed as in any way helpful. They were, indeed, directly the opposite.
May I say to the leader of the opposition that he has had a long and exceptional parliamentary experience. He spoke very often from this side of the house of the great burden which rests on the shoulders of a prime minister, and the need on the part of the Prime Minister for the cooperation of hon. members in all parts of the house. I hope the right hon. gentleman will keep that in mind now that he is on the other
side of the house. I shall welcome very much, the government will welcome, what he is able to give in the way of cooperation in dealing with the great problems which we have before us for consideration from day to day in these times. I hope that my right hon. friend will not again find it necessary to spend his time wholly in criticism or sarcasm, or in remarks that for the most part are facetious and in no way constructive or helpful.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon.
friends opposite are groaning a bit, but may I ask them just how, in seeking to be "helpful", their leader began his discourse yesterday. The first thing he did was to say that no doubt, as Prime Minister, I should find considerable difficulty in having so large a following. It was very natural that he should make a remark of that kind. Heaven knows with a very much smaller following he had enough difficulty to cope with all the time he was in office. The following he has behind him at the present moment is eloquent of the results of difficulties and discussions which he had at different times with sopae of his colleagues and members of his party.
The leader of the opposition was at particular pains to try to tell this house what had taken place during the formation of the present government. I heard him say repeatedly, when he was on this side of the house, that matters which pertained to the cabinet, and to his own party, were their business and nobody else's, and that it might be just as well for other people to mind their own business. I give him back his own words at this time. May I say that I think it ill became him, knowing the problems that face any first minister in the formation of a cabinet, to seek, at the very beginning of a parliamentary session, to create prejudice, not only as between different members of a party, but as between different parts of the country, by an appeal to race such as he sought to make in the remarks he offered at that time.

my right hon. friend's remarks are recorded on Hansard. Perhaps I may read to him just what he said. My right hon. friend intimated that one of my colleagues, who had been a colleague for many years, had gained the position that he now holds in the cabinet by "training his guns" on his leader. Does my right hon. friend deny that?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

But the little corporal from Sorel was not thus to be denied'. The support the party had

And then, bringing out the real point of the remark, which as I have said was intended to create racial differences if possible, my right hon. friend ended by saying:
In that position I am sure he will-
Referring to the present Minister of Public Works.
-in the words of the Minister of Justice, cast no reflection upon the people he represents and will discharge his great_ duties with fairness and with a sense of obligation that comes to one who is from a province that took the lead from 1930 and is now able to enforce its will upon the Prime Minister.
I ask if the remark, that one province in this country is able to force its will upon the Prime Minister, is not, in the relation mentioned, a deliberate effort on the part of the leader of the opposition to create prejudice against the province of Quebec.

When he says he does not know anything about this poster-

speechtext:
I guess my right hon. friend thought he would get out first. I have just been reminded that after my right hon. friend was out of sight other members of the party struck out the words "Vote Bennett " and had it read " Vote Conservative." Here is something that perhaps my right hon. friend does know a little about. Perhaps he will tell us he is incorrectly reported, but I find the following quotation which was sent pretty generally throughout Canada in the last week of the campaign, or at any rate very near the end of the campaign. Speaking at Sherbrooke-and I am sure my right hon. friend remembers that occasion-he said:
In the last session $1,000,000 had been voted as a stabilization fund to maintain the price to producers of dairy products. " I regret to say that the first cheques will not be paid until October 15 "-
The election was on October 14.
-Mr. Bennett continued, "and I hope that you farmers within the sound of my voice, when you get your cheques the day after the election, will not have qualms of conscience because you voted against the government that gave it to you."
That is, the government that gave these cheques out of a million dollar fund; the implication being that if the government changed their might be no cheques. Does my right hon. friend mean to imply that members on all sides of the house who had to do with voting

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
the appropriation that was made at that time were not entitled to any credit that might come from that appropriation?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was opposed by members of the opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, it was opposed and very rightly, for the reason that they were perfectly sure that my right hon. friend was putting through that million dollars for the purposes of an election, and no better evidence as to that could be adduced than I have pointed out. I might direct attention to other reports that were sent out, inspired or otherwise, to the effect that the bonus on wheat was expected to be paid on "Monday," the day of the elections, and so on. "Bribe" I think is not too strong a word-one bribe after another made to the electorate out of public funds by my right hon. friend himself. Yet he undertakes to find fault with some anonymous circular that he brings into the house for the purpose of creating racial prej udice.
That, Mr. Speaker, is not all. I think my right hon. friend knows something of the use to which the national radio was put by his party during the general election. I think he knows something about "Mister Sage" and his scurrilous and libelous, misrepresentations over the government-owned radio. Isay to my right hon. friend that as Prime Minister at that time he should not have permitted for one minute the use of the national radio in siudh a manner. He will have during the session plenty of chance to excuse himself on the score of what was permitted in that respect. It is true that there again his party sought to shield itself under anonymity. They had not the courage to come out and say who was supplying the money for these broadcasts. They had not the courage to say by whom they were written. They had not the courage or the honesty to say the broadcasts were political propaganda-propaganda of the worst type any party has ever put out, because it was most insidious in its nature and constituted an abuse in the use of national radio facilities during a political campaign. But he, as Prime Minister at the time, permitted all that to go on. I tell him now that that sort of thing will not continue under either the present or any other radio commission in Canada.
Let me come to the next matter to which my right hon. friend referred. He seemed to think it was an extraordinary thing that the speech from the throne should contain the following clause:
It is proposed to restore to parliament its control over taxation and expenditure by end-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
ing all measures which have deprived members of the House of Commons of this control, and which have served to invest the executive with unwarranted arbitrary powers.
My right hon. friend asked if there was ever anything so silly. Well, it shows how far, long continued practice may come to influence one's attitude of mind. I am perfectly sure that five years ago my. right hon. friend would not have sought to take away from parliament its control over taxation and expenditure and then tenm as silly an effort made to restore it. My right hon. friend asks what control was taken away. Well, I think that during the last parliament there was sufficient protest from the opposition side of the house against the use of the blank cheque and of the peace, order and good government clause of the relief legislation to enable him to know what is being restored at the present time. My right hon. friend knows very well that, as far as the control of taxation and expenditure is concerned, the only way in which this House of Commons can exercise that control is by having estimates brought down in connection with all public expenditures, and by having supply voted in the form of appropriations which give in detail the amounts required and the precise purpose for which moneys are to be used. I wonder if this country realizes how much money has been spent under the authority of the blank cheque, which was obtained every year from parliament under the allegation that it was needed to meet an emergent condition, and whioh was obtained in one instance under closure, and which would have had to be obtained in subsequent sessions in bhe same manner but for the desire of the opposition, not to prolong discussion in this house unduly.
Let me give the figures. The total expenditures made by order in council under the relief acts, which gave the government this blank cheque and other arbitrary powers, up to November I, 1935, just a few days after the present administration came into office, amounted to $192,000,000; in other words, more than the total expenditure of Canada in any fiscal year up to the fiscal year 1914-15, the year of the beginning of the Great war. That is to say, up to the time of the Great war this country's total expenditure had never equalled in any one year the amount of money that my right hon. friend paid out of the public treasury without appropriations during the time he was in office. Not a dollar of that amount was scrutinized in advance by hon. members of this house, or presented in a form in which it could be examined and voted upon.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Surely the right hon.
gentleman desires to say "annual."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Not a bit; I stand by every word I have said. More than that, loans amounting to 195,000,000 were made by my right hon. friend. This House of Commons was not asked to approve those individual loans. This House of Commons was treated as though it did not exist. The only people who received loans were those to whom the Prime Minister decided to give them between sessions and after parliament had prorogued.
But that was not all. Guarantees were given as well-guarantees to banks, to different interests of one kind and another, totalling how much, do you suppose, Mr. Speaker? On November first last, no less than $160,000,000. One railway company got a guarantee of $60,000,000 just about two days after parliament had prorogued. Not a word was said to parliament while it was in session about the necessity of giving any such guarantee to this road. Other guarantees were made on an extensive scale. I will not take time to put them on record, though I might well do so. The total amount of these guarantees outstanding on November first, however, is worth noting-$160,000,000. These are all obligations that have still for the most part to be met. In other words, in loans and guarantees and expenditures there was a total obligation upon the treasury of $447,000,000, or nearly half a billion dollars. Over the outlay of this vast sum the House of Commons as such had no real control. The people of Canada are talking about the size of the national debt, about the tremendous obligation there is on the shoulders of the people in the matter of taxation. Here is how $447,000,000 is accounted for. Will anyone tell me that any such liabilities would have been incurred if this House of Commons had had the right, which is its first right, a right and a duty above all other rights and duties of the House of Commons, to supervise in the most careful way every dollar of public expenditure?
I have in my hand an authoritative treatise on parliamentary grants by EHirell. Let me read a paragraph or two to illustrate the truth of what I have been saying as to the rights and duties of the House of Commons. I quote from page 3:
The most ancient, as well as the most valued, prerogative of the House of Commons is the right of supreme control over taxation, to which the right to control issues is a natural corollary. The prohibition of raising taxes without parliamentary authority would' be nugatory if the proceeds, even of legal taxes, could be
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
expended at the will of the sovereign. The right, therefore, of appropriation was a logical consequence of the right of levying supplies. The chain of historical evidence undeniably proves that a previous and stringent appropriation, often minute and specific, has formed an essential part of the British constitution.
All that was violated by my right hon. friend, not for one day but for every day for five years. Yet now he says: Isn't it a silly thing to suggest the restoration to the House of Commons of a power that will protect the rights of the people and enable the house to fulfil its constitutional duty to see that these rights are preserved? Let me give a further paragraph, as it appears at page 9:
The supreme control of the Commons over public grants, as already mentioned, necessarily demands the complete right of control over the manner in which those grants are spent. This second right must be inseparable from the first if the control over the grants is to be effective.
Yet, what did my right hon. friend say when we asked that the grants being made to the different provinces be audited by the auditor general? He said that to propose anything of the kind would be an insult to the provinces. Let me read only one more brief quotation, as it appears at page 18:
All the rules as to financial procedure are measures intended to protect the house against itself, to prevent hasty grants and ill-considered increases in the responsibilities of the people, while at the same time such rules are the best safeguard of the minority against the autocracy of the majority.
That is what we had during all of the last five years,-autocracy of the majority, and no real security or protection of the rights of the people themselves.
Of all the paragraphs in the speech from the throne, in my view the one which undertakes to restore to the House of Commons its control over the expenditure of public moneys is the most important of all. There was nothing which contributed so much to the return to this parliament of Liberal members in such large numbers as the knowledge on the part of the Canadian people that if we were returned we would see to it that once again the control by the House of Commons over expenditures and taxation would be duly and fully restored.
My right hon. friend next touched upon the textile inquiry. A little later in the day he took exception to any question being raised about the validity of certain laws which had been referred to the supreme court. He said he did not see why that matter had to be brought' up, and that it would have been much more fitting if the statutes could have operated a little while until trouble developed

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
somewhere and a suit was entered. However, when it comes to an inquiry into the conditions of employees in an establishment such as the one at Sherbrooke, when it comes to an investigation of the circumstances under which several hundred people without a day's notice were turned out in the middle of winter to shift for themselves, my right hon. friend says, "I wonder that the Minister of Justice did not see that that commission is unconstitutional."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, I did not say that; pardon me again. I said that I wondered if the Minister of Justice had looked into the question of the validity of it. I did not say it was or was not, and I gave the reference to the Manitoba case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am surprised that my right hon. friend was so keen to raise the point at all. If he had really been concerned with the well being of the employees of that great concern, and with the way in which the industry itself is carrying on, I think he would have been glad to see the inquiry proceed. The point I make is this: My right hon. friend was quite prepared to let the whole of his new deal legislation go into force at once' whether it was constitutional or otherwise, whether it was valid or invalid. Before the election he said, "I am so concerned with the well being of the working class in Canada that I do not care whether it is constitutional or not; I am going to see that this legislation is put on the statutes. Here, however, is one measure which is valid in every particular, and we find that at the first moment my right hon. friend is eager to take exception to the inquiry involved. If he had taken the trouble to look at the order in council-and I think he could have got it, if he had wished to have it, because I know he has a way of getting these documents from the privy council, whenever he wants them-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must
object to that statement. The statement is made that I have a method of getting documents from the privy council whenever I want them. The rule communicated to me by the Clerk of the Privy Council is that any orders in council passed during the five years we were in office he furnishes to me upon request, and that he had followed the same practice under the previous administration. I have received no document from the privy council' nor would I think of asking for any document of the privy council, except in the proper method, since the advent to office of this government. I must ask the right hon. gentleman to withdraw a statement which 12739- 6 J
would leave the impression that I had some method of getting from the privy council documents to which I was not entitled.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What my right hon. friend has stated bears out what I have said. He has stated that he thought his practice was a correct one, and I am not taking exception to it. He knows the correct method, and if he had wished to have a copy of the order in council, had he not already seen it, he had but to follow the correct method, which he himself has just mentioned.
May I say to the leader of the opposition that he may rest his mind as to the validity of the powers given this particular commission. The commission has powers respecting not only one industry, or one province or any particular concern in one province. The language is broad; perhaps I should read it:
The minister further observes that in order to determine the responsibility of employers and to enable appropriate action to be taken, not only with regard to safeguarding the interests of employees and of the public, but also of the industry itself, it is essential for the government to be fu/l'ly advised with respect to all matters surrounding the operations and conduct of the industries immediately concerned and interrelated and allied industries.
That takes into account not only the textile industry at Sherbrooke but the textile industries throughout Canada; do not let that be forgotten. Let us not forget that the concern at Sherbrooke intimated that its action in suddenly thrusting out great numbers of employees was due to an arrangement between this government and Japan. If any arrangement between the Canadian government and Japan is going to operate in that way with respect to any industry in Canada, the sooner we find out the facts of the situation, the better. We intend to go very fully into the whole position of the textile industries in Canada, and to consider competition not only from Japan but from Great Britain and everywhere else. The company in Sherbrooke said it was necessary to take such action to save the situation. In other words, it seemed to be necessary to deprive the employees of their wages. The commission will be interested in attempting to ascertain if, during the time the employees were deprived of their wages, the bonuses, salaries and the like of officers of the company were also cut off. My right hon. friend talks about-yes, what is it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I assume the right hon. gentleman in accordance with the rules will lay the order in council upon the table. Quotation by a minister from a public document necessitates its being laid upon the table.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, I shall lay It on the table, with pleasure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: So that we all may read it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes; it has already been published in the papers. Possibly the simplest method would be to place it on Hansard. My right hon. friend may then feel that we are trying to do full justice to the situation. It is as follows:
Certified to be a true copy of a minute of a meeting of the committee of the privy council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 27th January, 1936.
The committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 24th January, 1936, from the Minister of Finance, stating as follows:
On the 18th instant the following telegram, dated at Sherbrooke, Quebec, January the 18, 1936, and signed by Ant. Deslauriers, city clerk, on behalf of the city council of the city of Sherbrooke, was received by the Right Honourable the Prime Minister, and the Honourable the Minister of Finance:
" Special emergency meeting city council held to-day strongly ask that your government intervene immediately over the situation that has developed whereby our largest flat silk industries employing over a thousand hands has suddenly closed down leaving these people without employment Stop. Our city unable to cope with alarming situation and request your government take immediate steps to remedy this condition Stop. City cannot take care of such increased unemployment."
Also on the same date representations appeared in the press to the effect that according to word received from Sherbrooke uncertainty in the textile market, due in large part to Japanese competition in certain artificial silks, had forced the Dominion Textile Company to close its rayon plant at Sherbrooke, Quebec, and that the plant closed down would remain inactive until the present situation in the industry had been clarified. The Montreal Gazette of January 18, also contains the following relative to the foregoing representations:
"G. Blair Gordon. President of the Dominion Textiles, who is in the United States at present, last night confirmed the report in reply to a telegraph query. His message added ' Hope to reopen when we can see possibility of manufacturing goods which can be sold.' "
Upon receipt of the telegrams from the city council of Sherbrooke, an officer of the Department of Labour was immediately sent to Sherbrooke to report to the government upon the existing conditions. The report received by the government evidences the necessity, if the request of the city council of Sherbrooke is to be met and the present situation in the industry clarified, for investigation much more searching and extensive than is possible at the present time either by officials of any of the government departments or by the tariff board, and that it can most effectively be made by the appointment of a royal commission, clothed with powers to make the inquiry as searching and extensive as may be necessary.
The minister observes that the sudden cessation of operations in industrial establishments,

especially in the winter season, at a time of widespread unemployment, cannot fail to render more acute the distress and suffering of wage earners and their dependents, and also places upon municipalities and governments additional and unexpected financial burdens for relief. He is further of the opinion that industry generally and especially an industry which has had for years the benefit of the protection afforded by the customs tariff, should recognize its responsibility to carry on operations with due regard to its obligations to employees and to the public, and not to arbitrarily shut down its plants.
The minister further observes that in order to determine the responsibility of employers and to enable appropriate action to be taken, not only with regard to safeguarding the interests of employees and of the public, but also of the industry itself, it is essential for the government to be fully advised with respect to all matters surounding the operations and conduct of the industries immediately concerned and inter-related and allied industries;
That in this connection it is essential that full and complete information be available to the government covering a period of years with respect to costs, profits, wages, salaries and bonuses, tariff protection, investment, volume of production, and all other matters and things which together with information already available to the government will enable sound conclusions to be reached regarding the position of this and other branches of the textile industry in relation to British and foreign competition, and in particular, the extent to which the employer can reasonably and properly be expected to maintain employment over periods of temporary difficulty.
The minister recommends that for the purpose of making the said inquiry and examination, including the causes of the existing or any other such sudden cessation of industrial operations as may be referred to him, the Honourable W. F. A. Turgeon, of the Court of Appeal of Saskatchewan, be constituted a Royal Commissioner, under Part 1 of the Inquiries Act, Chapter 99 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. 1927, for the purpose of making such inquiry and examination, and that such commissioner have the special authority specified under part 3 of the said Act.
The minister further recommends that the commissioner be instructed to make his report as speedily as possible.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendations and submit the same for approval.
E. J. Lemaire,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
After having read the order in council, it is perhaps not necessary to table it, but I shall be very glad to do so if that is desired. I think the order makes perfectly clear the purpose and intention of the government.
My right hon. friend had a great deal to say last session about state intervention. Now that the election is over and an act of state intervention of the character set forth in this order in council is taken, he immediately busies himself with raising objection to the particular form of state intervention applied

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
in this instance. I am inclined to think this is the most effective form of state intervention possible with regard to those matters which affect the lives of human beings. If any industry thinks it is being adversely affected by any act of this government, all it has to do is to make known its desire to have a full inquiry made into the way in which its activities are being conducted, and it will get an inquiry with expedition.
We heard on the eve of the general election from more than one head of a great industry in this country-and I might have cited these instances had I felt inclined to do so this afternoon-that if a Liberal administration were returned and anything were done with respect to the tariff, there would be as a consequence an immediate shutting down of the industry involved, with consequent loss of Employment on the part of employees. In some instances, advertisements were circulated bearing upon them the names of the companies concerned, without question for the purpose of intimidating and of influencing their employees at the time of the general election. I gave my word at that time to the working men of this country that, if anything of that kind were attempted, it would not be long before the particular industry would be given every opportunity to show why it was necessary for it to take the action it did.
The day after this order in council was passed, the company at Sherbrooke found it possible to reopen. It issued a statement to the effect that, after all, it did not think the competition fr.om Japan was going to be so serious. I can imagine what we would have heard from my right hon. friend to-day if no action of that kind had been taken. I personally should not have been the least surprised to have seen the closing down of this particular industrial plant followed by several others. My right hon. friend would have waxed eloquent indeed on the effects of the arrangement made with Japan. But all he could say yesterday was that he would prophesy that two years hence we would be a sorry lot for having restored trade relations with a great country like Japan. He said that was only a prophecy, but he would make it nevertheless. Well, I do not take much stock in my hon. friend's prophecies. Five years ago he told the electors that he would end unemployment, but he had to admit yesterday that unemployment in Canada was worse at the time he went out of office than it had been at any other time in the whole of its history. In the circumstances, I do not think my right hon. friend's prophecies amount to very much.
Mr.. BENNETT: That is not what he said.

And there it ends; but, fortunately, the records of this House of Commons are kept where they are available to every hon. member, and we can see them for ourselves.
While on the question of our trade with Japan, may I say that the effect of the restoration of normal trade relations between Canada and Japan has been to put back to work thousands of men in the province of British Columbia and in other parts of this country. It has increased that purchasing power of which we have heard a good deal in recent years, which is so necessary to the people of Canada at this time. Instead of creating unemployment, it has been, along with another international agreement to which I shall refer a little later, a most important influence in helping to increase employment in industry, employment on the railways, and employment in many other directions.
My right hon. friend's next reference was to the legislation on unemployment. I shall not take up the time of the house at the moment in going into that question, because the bill itself will come before us very shortly. I should like, however, to direct attention to my right hon. friend's remarks with regard to the dominion-provincial conference, which discussed among other matters how most effectively the different provinces of the dominion and the municipalities might unite in solving the problem of unemployment. He said that he had never read a document so full of goodwill, so full of praise from one end to the other. May I tell my right hon. friend that good will is the basis of good work. The trouble with his administration in its relations with the provinces was that there never was a basis of good will. Good will is the thing above all others we have been seeking. We have it at last in this country as between the provinces and the dominion. Instead of ill will we have good will, in the effort to see what can be done to advance the commor interests of our country.

My right hon. friend also spoke about the wheat question. I am going to leave it to one of my colleagues to reply to him on this particular subject. All I want to say in a word is this, that, in nine and a half weeks following its appointment, the old board made net sales of only 12,500,000 bushels of wheat, whereas the new board, appointed on December 3, 1935, in the first six weeks of its operations, made net sales of 65,500,000 bushels. This accomplishment is all the more noteworthy, in 'that it was achieved without disturbing the price structure. May I here remind my right hon. friend of what he said last night as to his colleagues being fully informed on all ' mattem. I remember our waiting in this house, not for a few days or weeks, but for months, until the right hon. gentleman could be here, where I am ait this moment, and tell his colleagues as well as the house what he was going to do with respect to the matter of the sale of wheat.

The Bank of Canada was another subject to which reference was made. A MI is mentioned in the speech from the throne in connection with the Bank of Canada and it will be time enough to discuss that matter when we reach it.
As regards the reference to the supreme court of several enactments passed at the last session of parliament, the leader of the opposition criticized the Minister of Justice for having appointed counsel to 'Uphold the legislation I wonder what his criticism would have been if the Minister of Justice had appointed someone to oppose it. The Minister of Justice was kinder to my right hon. friend than I was prepared to be. I suggested to the minister that we ought to ask my right

hon. friend whether he would not accept a retainer, or, as he often generously acts without a retainer, w'hether he would not go before the supreme court and argue on behalf of his own legislation. The Minister of Justice said, however, that he thought that might put the right hon. gentleman in an embarrassing position. I must say I agreed with him, for if the legislation cou'ld noit be supported it would be indeed very embarrassing to the right hon. gentleman. I should, however, have liked to see my right hon. friend trying to defend that legislation before the court, and that for two reasons: In the first place, he would have done it very well, and in the second, I would wish him to feel that 'the desire of the present government was to give the legislation every possible opportunity thalt could be afforded to have its validity proved. That step at least has been taken, and I think my right hon. friend will agree with me that the government has adopted the right course in endeavouring to uphold to the utmost of its power the legislation which this parliament -put through. The fact that we have referred the legislation to the court, shows that we are carrying out what we had promised at the previous session we would do if we were returned to power.
I cannot agree with the leader of the opposition when he says that it would have been much better-nicer, I think' was the word he used-to have allowed all this legislation to remain on the statute books, until here and there actions were started and litigation commenced in the courts. I do not want to refer to a matter of domestic policy in another country, but I tMnk that possibly it is appropriate to call attention to the confusion and the difficulty that have arisen in the United States as a consequence of legislation which had been on the statute books and had been administered for a period of years being declared ultra vires by the supreme court. We have tried to avoid anything of the kind happening in Canada, and in doing so I believe we have taken an entirely right step.
There are only two other subjects to which I will refer before I conclude; they are the two which I imagine are uppermost in the minds of hon. members. The first is the Canada-United States trade agreement. That agreement will come up for very full discussion in the course of another few days. There is at the present time on the order paper a notice of motion which I have given asking the house to approve of the agreement. There will subsequently be introduced bills which will provide the necessary legisla-

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
tion for giving effect to all of its provisions. In due course, therefore, we shall have ample time to discuss the merits of this agreement.
What I wish to touch upon this afternoon is the impression which my right hon. friend sought last night to convey, that this agreement, so far as Canada is concerned, was the result of hasty and possibly immature action. He resented very strongly the fact that the government should have concluded, in something less than a month after its return to office, an agreement so far-reaching in its nature. He began by referring to the negotiations having extended over a period of weeks. He then reduced the period to days, and finally got down to the point where the agreement had been arrived at in an hour or two. If my right hon. friend had been aware of the facts he would have known that in those three weeks no government ever worked harder on any measure than did the present administration with respect to this particular agreement.
The mover of the address (Mr. Slaght) was kind enough yesterday to make special reference to myself in connection with the negotiation of that agreement. He gave to me personally all but exclusive credit. This I desire immediately to disclaim. There is no man in this House of Commons who is more conscious than I am of the fact that any power which the leader of a political party has comes in the main from his following. His power comes from the men and women who are his supporters and who have been his supporters through the years. If I have been able, in connection with the negotiation of this particular agreement, to play a part that has been helpful, I attribute it above all else to the fact that it was known, when I went to Washington, that for nearly seventeen years I had had the loyal and wholehearted support of the Liberal party-a party which from one end of Canada to the other had advocated a reciprocal agreement with the United States -and that at no time had the leader of any other government in this dominion behind him such a following as I had at the time I began the negotiation of the agreement. In other words, there was a guarantee at once that we were in earnest; that we meant business, and that we were in a position to carry out effectively what we might undertake to do.
Contrast the position of my right hon. friend? He had a couple of years within which to show his bona fides. He had all the time required to make perfectly clear what his following would do, what he was able to do, yet weeks, months, years slipped by, with nothing or very little in the way of
negotiation on his own part. Toward the end of last year there came the document which my right hon. friend put on Hansard last night. If that document meant anything, why did he not continue to proceed on the basis of negotiations that was laid down in it? He did not need to place that document on Hansard in order to have it known. He took good care to give it to the electorate at the beginning of the recent campaign. He took good care throughout the campaign to have it more or less inferred that he had been negotiating on the right lines: he was going to get concessions on lumber, on fish, on cattle, on milk and cream; he was going to get concessions on potatoes; he was going to get concessions on other things. It was all set out in this particular document. But in order to get it, it was necessary for him to get back into power. Now, was not that the fact?

Well, let us see what my right hon. friend said at that time and see how his words would impress the government of the United States when my right hon. friend went to negotiate an agreement with them, or how they would impress the Canadian people as to his belief in the wisdom of an agreement of the kind. Speaking in this house on November 20, 1911, my right hon. friend said:

Mr. Speaker, the risk was real and the danger imminent. I doubt not that when the proposals to which I have referred were first introduced, they were regarded merely as trade proposals; but when it was ascertained that in their ultimate results they involved the whole future of Canada, then it was that the national spirit of our people was aroused. I venture to think that the right hon. gentleman who so successfully leads the opposition in this house would not have introduced those proposals if he could have foreseen that there would have arisen around them an agitation, the results of which were so vital to the imperial and national future of the country. While I mention the name of the right hon. gentleman, may I be permitted to tender to him my sincere congratulations upon his having attained another anniversary of his natal day, with the expression of the hope that he may be long spared faithfully and illustriously to serve the state in the position which he at present occupies.
Mr. Speaker, in that portion of this great dominion in which I am privileged to reside, a very substantial portion of our population has come from the great republic to the south, and one of the strongest reasons I had for opposing the reciprocity agreement was that it threw into the melting pot for solution a question that involved a problem in patriotism. When we remember that so large a portion of our population came from that great republic, where they inherited traditions that were at least not favourable to monarchial institutions; when they learned through the medium of the American press, that, however much their former political parties differed with each other, they showed unanimity in favour of these proposals, and when they found American public men preaching a doctrine that indicated that the consequences of this agreement would be the absorption of western Canada at least by the great republic, and at all events rendering impossible for all time the commercial and organic union of those overseas dominions and the motherland which comprise the British Empire, it was little wonder that these people allied themselves with those who were in favour of the reciprocity pact. But it is a pleasure for me to say on behalf of these new settlers that as soon as they discovered that the Canadian people were not in favour of the agreement, they responded to the prevailing sentiment, and made it apparent that they proposed to devote their time and energies to the upbuilding of this great country just as they had done in the land from which they came; and, as they are settlers who are accustomed to pioneer conditions, they are enabled, now that this question is settled for ever, to assist us in laying the foundations of a great state.
The question "settled forever"! No reciprocity with the United States as long as my right hon. friend had anything to do with it. That is the explanation of the remarks made by the present Postmaster General1 (Mr. Elliott) in the course of the last campaign: that it would be impossible for my right hon. friend to negotiate an agreement with the United States. Anyone who had declared

himself in those terms, and said he still held to them, would find it impossible to make a reciprocity agreement.
May I give another reason why there was strong cause for supposing that my right hon. friend would never succeed in negotiating an agreement. The people, not of this country alone but of other countries, know how he negotiated the Canada-United Kingdom agreement, and the kind of negotiator he was at that time.
Not bad.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Not bad! It could not have been worse. I am not speaking for the moment of the terms of the agreement; I am speaking of the methods of my right hon. friend in negotiating it. It was generally known as well that my right hon.. friend had gone out of his way to help to create, or at least to prolong, a trade war with another great country, Japan. One who thinks in terms of economic nationalism, who advocates that we must have at least some form of commercial conflict with other nations, is not likely to be the person whom any country is going to trust and in whom it will have faith when it comes to the negotiation of a trade agreement.
I was more than amazed when I heard the leader of the opposition suggest that the President of the United States, while negotiating with him, might be a party to an agreement with another political party in this country. I was amazed that he could even think of such a thing. I am sure the president must be relieved that his government did not get very far with my right hon. friend, if that is the sort of view he entertains with respect to the responsibilities of one holding the highest position in his land. It was not worthy of my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

Now, Mr. Speaker, I will have to raise the question. The question of order, neatly put, is this: Has any speaker the right to misrepresent a statement made by another? It is represented that I suggested yesterday that the President of the United States had some form of arrangement or agreement with the right hon. gentleman with respect to a trade agreement. I stated yesterday positively that I did not hold any such view and could not possibly hold any such view. I do suggest to you, sir, that the right hon. gentleman must not be permitted to make statements containing three-quarters of the truth and then make statements that are wholly inaccurate with respect to what I have said. I call upon the chair to say to the speaker, whoever he may be, that he must not
attribute to other members statements they did not make.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

On the point of order, if it be such, may I read what my right hon. friend said last night as reported in Hansard at page 60:
The Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott), in the speeches delivered during the campaign, said that the President of the United States would not negotiate with the Bennett government, and the Prime Minister of this country said that he would negotiate a treaty in ninety days. Does that mean that they had an arrangement that no agreement was to be made with that government, or does it mean this-
Mr. Mackenzie King: Shame.
Mr. Bennett: I beg your pardon?
Mr. Mackenzie King: I say "shame" to the right hon. gentleman when he insinuates that a government with which he was dealing would enter into such an arrangement with another government.
Mr. Bennett: That is what I am trying to say.
Mr. Mackenzie King: And I say, "Shame."
And I repeat it at this moment.

Mr. Bennett: ... and I decline to believe that the government of tihe United States was a party to any arrangement that would reflect upon itself. I say, shame; I agree with the Prime Minister; but the shame is to those who went about the country and tried to induce the people to believe that the United States would not carry on negotiations with the Conservative government of the day, but that there had to be a change of government to make a bargain with the United States. say.

speechtext:
Very well,
I shall not seek to say more. Let me say to my right hon. friend that I feel very much relieved that he now repudiates what he said yesterday, and that he has made it perfectly clear, that as the leader of a political party in this country,-he was not insinuating that the President of the United States had entered into an agreement with some other party while
