negotiating with my right hon. friend. I accept my right hon. friend's statement; I am very happy to accept it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Once more I have to say-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen opposite may have a huge majority, but the rules of this house are going to be observed. We have rights in this chamber, and hon. gentlemen opposite may as well begin to understand that through force of numbers and power they are not going to take from us, however small we may be, any of our rights. My point is this: At page 61 I said yesterday positively that I made no such statement, that I declined to believe any such statement. When the right hon. gentleman says he accepts my statement of to-day, that was simply the statement I made yesterday, and the right hon. gentleman has no right thus to misstate what I said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to leave myself and the leader of the opposition in the judgment of the house and to allow the English language to speak for itself.
What I really desired more particularly to tel! the house is something of the nature of the negotiations which took place. As I have said, my right hon. friend has done his utmost to create the impression that the agreement was reached in a hasty manner and without due consideration. The present administration was returned to office on October 23. October 24 was Thanksgiving day. I attended Thanksgiving service in the morning and like a good many others, in expressing my thanks to providence for its many blessings, I included thanks for the country's deliverance from the government which for the five previous years had been in office. In the afternoon of that very first day of office, I called on the United States Minister to Canada, Mr. Norman Armour. I told Mr. Armour that I had come at once to confer with him because my colleagues and I regarded as the most important of all the questions before the people of Canada that of the negotiation of a trade agreement between the United States and Canada. I asked Mr. Armour if he would assist me in arranging an interview with the President of the United States at the earliest possible moment.
On the following day in council my colleagues and I immediately began to go over the whole matter of trade negotiations between Canada and the United States. As my right hon. friend very rightly said yesterday,

everything that could be known with respect to the effect of the United States tariff upon Canada, and of the Canadian tariff upon the United States, and what was possible in the way of an agreement, within certain limits, had been worked out with great care by the members of the public services of this country and of the United States. All that ground had been gone over during the preceding year or two, and the information was immediately available to the administration. Most of it, not all, but a good part of it, had been available to my right hon. friend for nearly a year before. It naturally also became available to my colleagues and myself the moment we came into office. I want to be the first to express my appreciation of all that was done in a preliminary way, and done with great efficiency and exceptional skill, by the officials of the public service of this country.
We went over all the material very carefully. We had many meetings of council dealing with the question. What was even more to the point my colleagues the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) along with myself were constituted a committee of the cabinet to go very fully, and in detail, along with members of the service into the different matters which had to do with the questions that would come up in discussion with the United States. Within a day or two after we had gone over the ground with the officials here and had seen, as far as it was permissible to see, what had been placed before our predecessors in office, we immediately sent the officials of the Departments of External Affairs, Finance, Trade and Commerce, and National Revenue, who had been dealing with these matters, to Washington to get into touch with officials in the United States. We pointed out what concessions we were prepared to make, and what concessions we thought we ought to obtain. After our officials had taken up matters there with officials of the United States government, keeping in touch with our government over the long distance telephone and also by telegraph, as the United States officials were keeping in touch with their government, I went to Washington myself to have the interview with the president which had previously been arranged for the earliest possible date. My right hon. friend says that the press stated that I was leaving Ottawa on account of my health. I do not think the press said anything about my health; I believe it was said that I was going to take

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
a short vacation largely to get a chance to think over many matters after having had a very strenuous time in opposition, in a general election and in the formation of the government. I do not believe any one in the country thought that was anything out of the way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But may I say this; I was determined to take no vacation until I was perfectly satisfied it was going to be impossible to effect a beneficial agreement with the United States or until an agreement had been secured. I might immediately upon the formation of the government have gone on a vacation. I admit I was pretty tired at the time, but I felt the important thing for the people of Canada, and the most important of all the immediate duties of the government, was to see if we could work out a mutually beneficial trade agreement with the United States. I knew that every day that passed was going to make it more difficult to effect an agreement. We all know that as a government approaches the time of a general election it is more difficult for it to carry on negotiations. We all know that as a government is about to meet its parliament or congress, its ministers and others are more busily engaged than at other seasons, and with congress about to assemble the first week of January, with the general election coming in the United States this year, I believed there was not a moment to be lost, and my colleagues felt the same. We therefore devoted our time to the work of this agreement to the exclusion of everything else that it was possible to exclude.
It is not the number -of years, it is not the number of months that are taken to do a thing; it is the intensity of effort and the will and determination given to a task that count in negotiations of this sort. As I have said, every hour, every moment of my time and much of the time of most of my colleagues was occupied with these matters until the day I went to Washington to confer with the president, and pretty much all thereafter until I returned to sign the agreement. When I was fortunate enough to meet the president our talks together were in the nature of interviews finally to determine what could and would be done. Every phase of the situation had, as I have already said, been reviewed with the departments of government in the United States by their own ministers, matters had been reviewed with the different departments here by our ministers, I mean the departments
immediately concerned with the questions involved in the agreement, and then by the cabinet as a whole. Before I left, we knew exactly what we were prepared to do. There were a few matters outstanding. These matters had an important bearing upon any final arrangement that might be made. It was these matters that above all others I had to discuss with the President of the United States.
After I had had my conference with the president, the committees which had been active here and in Washington came together again and worked as hard as they possibly could, night as well as day, until finally we were able to iron out all the difficulties that had presented themselves up to that time, and to reach the terms of a final agreement on the night of Saturday, November 9. My colleagues knew how far I was at liberty to go before I left. I wished to make perfectly sure that they would know every detail before the final agreement was effected. I therefore returned to Ottawa immediately after reaching the point where I had an agreement in such form that it simply awaited the approval of the government here, having had the approval of the government of the United States before I left. I asked members of council to meet me early Monday morning November 11, which was Armistice day. I do not often do public work on Sunday, but I did ask two or three of my colleagues to meet me on my return to Ottawa on Sunday night, the Minister of Finance, the Minister' of Trade and Commerce and the others I have mentioned, so that I might at that stage go with them in detail into the different points that had come up for further consideration. When the cabinet met on Monday we were in a position in a very short time to give our unanimous consent to the agreement which had been arrived at. Thereafter it had to be put into final shape for formal signature, a not inconsiderable task in itself. I mention these things in order to make it perfectly clear that the agreement as it was arrived at was the result, first of all, of the work which had been done by members of the public service of Canada, work which had been done in part under the auspices of my right hon. friend, and the importance of which I wish to be the first to acknowledge; work which was materially aided, may I say, by the legations both here and in Washington. And that is another feature I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members. I do not believe it would have been possible to have made such an agreement in so short a time but for the good will which prevailed on the part of our

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
friends in the United States. legation here, the good will which prevailed towards the United States on the part of our representatives at Washington, and the faot that in these legations we were able to come into immediate touch with- each other personally at a moment's notice instead of having to negotiate by correspondence.
I leave the matter there. When we come to the discussion of the agreement itself I shall then discuss its merits. But may I say to the house at this moment, that I believe the agreement which has been reached between the United States and Canada is one which will be productive of infinite good to both countries. I shall go further and say that I believe the action taken by the United States and Canada in negotiating this agreement will help to make for a better condition of things in other countries and other parts of the world. During these last few years the different countries of the world have been going mad through basing their actions on a false doctrine of economic nationalism, through having nothing to do with their neighbours, regarding trade as a species of warfare, instead of a matter of mutual interest. This agreement marked an improvement in that position, a complete change to another direction. I believe we will live to see the day when this agreement between the United States and Canada, will be held up as marking a new beginning in the relations between the countries of the world; a new beginning in the direction of more in the way of trade and of international friendship; and of less in the way of those things which make for ill to the world at large.
Before concluding I desire to say a word on the question of sanctions arising out of the Italo-Ethiopian war, and Article XVI of the Covenant of the League of Nations. Here again, I wish to reserve until a more appropriate time the discussion which this house will doubtless desire to have upon that subject. All that I shall deal with at the moment is the inference which I thought my right hon. friend sought to convey yesterday that Doctor Riddell, who is the advisory officer of the government at Geneva, in having proposed that oil and some other commodities should be added to those already included in the economic sanctions against Italy, was acting under instructions from the present [DOT] administration. My right hon. friend went out of his way to say that he had had long experience with Doctor Riddell, and that he could think of no officer who had been more careful in the matter of taking directions from his government, who had been more punctilious

about telegraphing for instructions and the like than Doctor Riddell had been. I am sure the impression left on the minds of those who heard my right hon. friend was that Doctor Riddell, with respect to this all important matter, at least must have communicated with the government and received substantial instructions from the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Quite the opposite.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In order to make I he position clear may I give the house very briefly the main stages which have to be taken into account in considering this question of sanctions.
On October 7, 1935, the Council of the League of Nations concurred in the conclusion of the Committee of Six that Italy had resorted to war in disregard of its covenants. On October 11, 1935, the assembly of the league passed a resolution taking cognizance of the action of the council, calling attention to article 16 and recommending the establishement of a coordination committee to advise on sanctions to be applied. Between October 11 and October 19 the committee of coordination recommended the imposition of four economic and financial sanctions. Between the same dates, October 11 and October 19-all the dates are of course, in 1935-the Canadian delegation to the League of Nations concurred in the assembly resolution and participated in the committee discussion and recommendations. I ask you to notice, Mr. Speaker, that all the dates to which I have thus far referred were during the time my right hon. friend was Prime Minister and while his government was in office. The present administration did not take office until October 23. Prior to October 23, in fact as late as October 19, the Canadian delegation, the delegation which my right hon. friend had appointed and to which he had been giving instructions, concurred in the assembly resolution and participated in the committee discussions and recommendations.
When the present government took office we were immediately confronted with the recommendations of the committee, and our first duty was to say whether Canada would carry out these recommendations, whether we would apply sanctions with respect to the export of arms, credits to Italy, imports from Italy and the export of certain key products to Italy. On October 29 I issued a statement to the effect that Canada would apply these sanctions. The sanctions were enforced by Canada on the following dates:	Embargo
on the export of arms, October 31, 1936; prohibition of credits to Italy, November 15,

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
1935; embargo on imports from Italy, November 15, 1935; embargo on exports of certain key products to Italy, November 15, 1935.
That in a word is the whole story, apart from the feature to which special reference was made by my right hon. friend. He said that the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who was acting Prime Minister during the time I was absent, was wrong in having issued a statement to the effect that the proposal to impose an oil sanction was not the proposal of the government of Canada but was one which had been made by Doctor Riddell on his own responsibility. Let me say at once that I take full responsibility for what the acting Prime Minister did and said during the time of my absence. I would do so in any event; but I do so particularly because before taking the action he did my hon. friend and colleague communicated with me in Georgia where I was on vacation, and I expressly stated to him that I thought he should inform the people of Canada that the action with respect to oil sanctions taken at Geneva, which was being stated by the press to have been the action of the government of Canada, was not in fact the action of the government of Canada but that of the committee of the league itself.	[DOT]
That is the whole story, except as to whether or not it was a fact Doctor Riddell acted on his own authority or was acting under instructions from the government. Let me say at once that I agree with my right hon. friend when he says that Doctor Riddell is a very efficient public servant. I think on many occasions he has rendered Canada admirable service at Geneva. I have reason to believe that up to the time about which I am to speak he had been scrupulously careful about waiting until he had received instructions before taking action. I must say that having held that opinion of him, I had full confidence that nothing would be done at Geneva which might be construed as having been done in the name of Canada which the government of Canada itself had not authorized in the first instance. What was my amazement when on reading a morning paper I found that Doctor Riddell at Geneva was reported to have proposed to add oil, coal and steel to the list of commodities which by sanctions were to be prohibited from export to Italy. No instructions whatever had been sent to him authorizing anything of the kind. I immediately asked the under secretary of state if he could throw any light on the matter. I ascertained that a communication had come from Doctor Riddell
, saying that a question was likely to be raised at the league, with respect to the particular commodities to which I have referred, and asking what he was to do with respect to them. I recalled then having had this partir cular point mentioned and having directed that word was immediately to be sent that no action of any kind was to be taken by Doctor Riddell without specific instructions from the government. I asked whether that communication had been sent, and was informed that it had been sent within an hour after receipt of the communication from Doctor Riddell. So that so far as the present administration is concerned I say we gave specific direction to Doctor Riddell that he was to do nothing in, the matter of extending sanctions without express direction from the government itself.
What was the date of the motion made by Doctor Riddell at the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It was not a motion; it was only a suggestion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I believe I can ascertain the date, but may I say to the hon. member that it was a suggestion or motion made in the committee of coordination. Speaking from memory I believe the date was either November 2 or November 4, but I shall seek to advise the hon. member accurately.
Was the date of that suggestion by Doctor Riddell prior to the statement of the right hon. gentleman to the effect that he and his government were in favour of sanctions?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have already stated that the government's action on sanctions was made public by myself on October 29. It was November 2 or November 4, I am not positive as to the date that Doctor Riddell took the action to which I have referred.
Would Doctor Riddell's action at the League of Nations be equivalent to carrying out the intention of the government as expressed by the statement of the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No; the action of the government had specific reference to an embargo on the export of arms, the prohibition of credit to Italy, the embargo on imports from Italy, and the embargo on certain key products to Italy, all of which were definitely named and set forth, and had been decided upon by the committee of coordination at Geneva.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
May I say to my right hon. friend, because [DOT] I understand his difficulty in appreciating the situation, that the committee of coordination at Geneva was not a League of Nations committee in the sense in which I have no doubt he regards it. It was not a committee of the assembly nor a committee of the council. It was a committee of representatives of different countries represented at Geneva who took under review the question of deciding what particular sanctions the different countries that were representatives of the league would agree upon. This committee set up a further committee of eighteen.

Was not that committee
set up by the council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: By the president of the committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The president himself named this subcommittee of the coordination committee.

It was action agreed upon
by the council, I understand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall not
contradict my hon. friend at the moment, but I am pretty sure I am right and that he is mistaken, and that it was not a committee that was approved formally by the council at all. However, the committee as I say took under review from October 11 to 19 in the manner I have described the question of what particular sanctions should be applied, and sought to ascertain through communication with the different governments reipresented at the league whether or not they would be agreeable to these particular sanctions. When ' agreement was found to exist between practically all the countries that were members of the league, then the different countries were notified of the decision that it would be desirable to have the sanctions imposed, and each country took its own action on its own authority, as my right hon. friend yesterday said it was its duty to do. In other words, there bad been a violation of the covenant and the different members of the league had an obligation to impose certain penalties as a result of that particular violation.
Would the right hon. gentleman explain what Doctor Riddell said or did or moved or suggested?-because there is some doubt in my mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am coming to that. Doctor Riddell's statement of what he said was this. He had understood that the question of adding oil, coal, iron, copper-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Steel.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: -steel and one or two other commodities was to come up for consideration on a particular day-I think it was November 3-and he sent a telegram stating that the question was likely to come up and asking for instructions. The answer was sent to him, as I have said, within an hour after this communication had been received, telling him to take no action at all, to exercise no initiative in any way in a matter of the kind; to wait for instructions from the government before acting on any of these matters. It so happened that within a very short time after Doctor Riddell had sent his first cable the question came up, wholly he says unexpectedly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In the committee. He had thought it would be another day or two before it would come up, but coming up in this unexpected way he did not wait until he had received an answer to his first cable but took it upon himself to make the proposal that oil and certain other commodities should be added to the list of articles which were to be prohibited export to Italy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Was it a suggestion or a proposal, may I ask the right hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think possibly much depends upon the value to be attached to either word. It was a suggestion; it was a proposal; I take the terms as being more or less synonymous. What I want to bring out very clearly is this, that Doctor Riddell as regards the action he took says, and I think quite rightly, that he was not in any sense to be regarded as acting for Canada, that he was simply acting as a member of a committee on which he had been asked to serve and on which he had been working with other members.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And whose proceedings were private, as I understand it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand that the proceedings, as my right hon. friend says, were private or rather were supposed to be private. May I say this, which I think should be made quite clear with respect to the question of oil being added to the list of sanctions. That matter had been proposed before Doctor Riddell proposed it, by one of the European countries. As a matter of fact, from what he says to me, it seemed to have been taken for granted generally that oil would be included in the sanctions, and

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
apparently oil received at that time very little in the way of discussion or consideration at all. The discussion took place more particularly in reference to copper and in reference to derivatives of natural products. There sSems to have been a difference of view between members as to whether the sanctions should be confined to natural products or whether they should also include derivatives, and in order, as it were, to equalize the matter between the different countries Doctor Riddell as a member of the committee says that he made the suggestion he did, and made it with the best of intentions and in all good faith.
That I think is the whole story. I believe that Doctor Riddell thought he was doing what was right, that his intentions were entirely right. I do not criticize him on that score at all, but I do say that he had no authority and no right to take any step that was at all likely to be of importance in a critical situation such as there was in Europe at that time without specific instructions and authority from the government of Canada, especially as it was impossible to have the action he took at Geneva interpreted otherwise than as part of the action of the government of this country. When the statement appeared the government immediately communicated with Doctor Riddell and reprimanded him for the action he had taken. He was told in plain language that he had exceeded his authority, that he should not have taken the step he did, and that he was not to take any further action without most careful and full instructions. I have since so expressed myself to Doctor Riddell in Ottawa. On receipt of the government's cable Doctor Riddell immediately cabled back regretting that he had by his action embarrassed the government. I think he embarrassed more than the government. I think his action served to embarrass the country as a whole, and to embarrass to some extent, although it may have been well intended, the whole situation in Europe.
My right hon. friend says that we should not have taken any further step in the matter. May I say that when we became aware of Doctor Riddell's statement and of what he had done, we considered very carefully whether we should not immediately publicly repudiate his act, and it was only because we were most anxious not to take any step which might possibly embarrass the situation in Europe or which might appear even remotely to indicate an exception on the part of Canada to what was being done by other parts of the British empire, that we refrained from taking any action of that
kind. In addition to that we were anxious to hear from Doctor Riddell himself the circumstances surrounding his action and to know fully from him what it was that caused him to take the action he did. We wanted to know all the circumstances pertaining thereto. For these reasons-and I think they were good reasons, wise reasons-nothing further was said at the time about the matter.
If other countries had referred, as they should have done, to the action taken at that time by the committee as the action of a committee and not as the action of any member of the committee or of any particular country, or government, nothing further would need to have been said. But the situation wholly changed when after a short time the press of England and of Europe began to refer from day to day to the proposed application of an oil sanction as the especial desire of the government of Canada, and gave to it the designation of the Canadian proposal, and when representatives of the British and other governments at Geneva were being told that the proposal was Canada's proposal and that they should hasten their action because Canada was anxious and insistent in the matter. I do not know whether hon. members realize the extent to which that impression was being created throughout Europe. Let me read some of the references as they appeared in the British press. The News Chronicle of November 4 has the following:
Far the most interesting event at Saturday's sitting of the committee was Canada's proposal that the list of key products to be barred to Italy should be extended so as to include oil, petrol, coal, iron and steel. We hope this body will proceed at once to examine and report upon how far general acceptance can be obtained for the Canadian proposal.
And on November 5:
The ban on these exports proposed by the new Liberal government of Canada will not come into force ... until the conditions exist for making effective. The proposal originally made by Canada to place an embargo on these and other products ...
The Morning Post of November 5 carried the following:
Oil and coal sanctions. Canada's proposal discussed.
The Canadian proposal is in a way the touchstone of the practical value of economic sanctions.... It is also of interest that Chile made certain reservations this morning on the Canadian proposal.
I quote next from the Observer of November 4:
Canada's new proposal. Serious effect on Italy.
The most important proposal before the
committee of eighteen to-day came from Canada, who brought forward the suggestion that

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
petroleum and its derivatives, coal, iron, cast iron and steel, be added to the list of banned exports to Italy.
Mr, CAHAN: Are these cables from Geneva or are they editorial comments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
These are articles which appeared in the newspapers of England. I have quoted from the News Chronicle, the Morning Post and the Observer. I will give one from the Daily Telegraph of November 4:
Ban on coal and oil urged. Canada's move at Geneva.
Canada, supported by Great Britain, to-day proposed that exports to Italy and to Italian possessions of oil and its by-products, coal, cast iron and steel, should be prohibited.
Next I quote from the London Spectator of November 22:
No rapid results can be looked for unless the extension of the list of key products proposed by Canada is agreed on.
And on November 29:
Canada, very properly dissatisfied with a list of key commodities from which the master key was absent, proposed that petrol and coal should be added, provided that the non-league states were willing to cooperate.
These articles lion, gentlemen will I think agree, are not at all uncertain in the emphasis they place on the proposal being one, not of an individual, not of a committee, but of the government of Canada, and of the present federal government as distinguished from all preceding governments.
It is simply an exemplification of Geneva politics.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows a good deal about that, and he can speak with some degree of authority.' He has asked about dispatches from Geneva. I have one or two which I might read and which appeared in our own Canadian newspapers. I quote the following dispatch from Geneva, dated November 5, which came through the Associated Press:
An official communique said a Canadian proposal adopted by the sub-committee provided that the list of "key products" barred to Italy should be extended by various articles "as goon as conditions necessary to render this extension effective have been realized."
Then there is a dispatch dated London, November 26, by the Canadian Press:
Official quarters mentioned that Britain already agreed in principle to the proposal at Geneva of Doctor W. A. Riddell of Canada, that coal and oil be added to the list of products not to be sent to Italy, when such an embargo could be made effective.

Then there is a dispatch from Geneva, November 26, Canadian Press-Havas:
League of Nations circles believed to-night an oil embargo against Italy will go into effect early in December, in conformity with Canada's proposal to the League sanctions committee.
I might quote a great many more, but I think that what I have quoted is sufficient to show why, when the press, not only of England and Europe but of all the countries of the world, began to refer to the matter of the application of oil sanctions as Canada's proposal, a proposal of the Canadian government, the time had come, having regard to the critical situation that was known to exist at that moment in Europe, to make very clear, so far as Canada was concerned, that it was not Canada's proposal, that it was not the Canadian government's proposal, but that it was simply the proposal of an individual member of a committee and should have been known, if it was to be designated at all as a proposal, as that of the committee which had been appointed to review these matters.
What did Sir Samuel Hoare say, speaking as Foreign Secretary in the British House of Commons, as to how this particular proposal should have been designated? I quote from a report that appears in the London Times of December 6, 1935:
As to the embargo upon oil, about which there has been so much public discussion, I need only say that, as in the whole field of collective action, so in this particular part of it, we are prepared to play our part. The League has already agreed to the embargo in principle. Great Britain has already agreed to it in principle. I should like to make it quite clear that no one government is any more responsible than another for this collective decision, or indeed for any of the sanctions proposals. These proposals are put forward by subcommittees on which many governments are represented. They are laid before the Committee of Eighteen on the responsibility of the Whole subcommittee from which they come.
If that statement had been made some time before, it would not have been necessary for the Minister of Justice, in my absence, to make a statement which I would have made myself had I been here; but it was after the statement was made by the Minister of Justice, making perfectly clear that this proposal was not the proposal of the Canadian government or, in any particular of Canada., but was the proposal of the committee, that the British Foreign Secretary at the time saw the wisdom and the desirability of making that abundantly plain to everyone in Europe and elsewhere, wherever his utterance might reach.
What my hon. colleague the Minister of Justice did was exactly what the British Foreign Secretary did in the statement I have

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
read. He issued a statement of fact, which made it perfectly clear, without commenting in any way at all on the merits of the proposal, but dealing exclusively with its origin, that this sanction proposal was not a Canadian proposal but was one of the committee of the league. He simply stated the truth.
Now I ask hon. members of this house: do they think it was not desirable for the Canadian government to make the truth perfectly clear, particularly at the time? After all apart from other considerations there is such a thing as a sense of proportion in international affairs as in all else. Do hon. members think that it is Canada's role at Geneva to attempt to regulate a European war and to say what other countries are to do with respect to the manner in which a European was is to be carried on? I think it appalling to contemplate the possible consequences of even such action being taken by any representative of this country in Geneva; and not desiring that Canada should appear in any such light or be placed in any such light, the government took good care to make clear the position, as it did.

Is there any difference between the responsibility of a suggestion being made by a member of this committee, who happened to be the representative of Canada, and subsequent acquiescence in and approval of the whole report or proposal of the committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a very great deal of difference, and my hon. friend knows there is. The question of approval is a matter for consideration. I am glad my hon. friend has interrupted me, because it will help to make the matter quite clear in an all important particular which is evidently in his mind and of which I have not spoken as yet. The question of oil sanctions has not yet been approved. There is as yet no acquiescence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: By anybody?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
By anybody. I cannot make that too clear, that whether there will be an actual application of oil sanctions remains yet to be considered. When that proposal comes before this country, if it does come, it will be considered on its merits. Up to the present time there has been no proposal for application made and there has been no acquiescence in any proposed application. What we wished to make perfectly clear was the exact position of Canada with regard to the origin of a proposal which is still being considered.
May I add this: my right hon. friend has
referred to what he read in a paper as he went through the Panama canal about the action of-

May I interrupt? I was
probably mistaken, because I was away myself, and what I read I read in the papers. But I understood that after this suggestion had been made in committee, and made public, the leading nations, England, France, others, concurred in this sanction being applied, the only reservation being an inquiry as to the time and circumstances under which it should be applied.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: After the committee had considered this matter they communicated with different countries to ascertain whether they would approve an oil sanction. My hon. friend is right in saying that countries were circularized to that effect, but few replied.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The subcommittee of the co-ordinating committee actually reported in favour of it, and had the statement made by Sir Samuel Hoare been made by the Minister of Justice I do not think anyone could have made any complaint. But it was the terms in which the statement was made that I was speaking of yesterday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Now my right hon. friend is changing his ground entirely. It is now a question of the terms. I am very glad, however, to have my right hon. friend, say that all he objected to was the terms in which the matter was referred to rather than the matter itself. I am very glad to know that that is my right hon. friend's view. In other words, he thinks it was wholly proper that the government of Canada should have made a statement similar to that which was made by Sir Samuel Hoare, and which made it perfectly clear that this proposal was not Canada's proposal or the Canadian government's proposal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think what should have been done was exactly what Sir Samuel Hoare did-to say that any of these proposals emanating from the subcommittee in the report to the main committee were the proposals, not of any government, but of the subcommittee reporting to the committee. I think that would have been the proper thing. But it was vastly different from what was said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When I was interrupted-

I beg pardon. I was simply seeking information.

98	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I know that my hon. friend is always more than polite, particularly towards myself. May I say that when for the moment I stopped speaking I was referring to what the leader of the opposition said with regard to the effect on his mind of what he read in a paper as he was going through the Panama canal; the fact that something had been said in an Italian paper, drawing its own inferences and conclusions from the statement that had been issued at Ottawa. I would like to ask my right hon. friend and other hon. members of this house, knowing the very critical condition of affairs in Europe at that time, and that, by pressing the matter of oil sanctions at that stage, a situation might have arisen in Europe the like of which has not been known since the great war, whether this government would have been kept free from criticism if it had not made known that this was not a Canadian proposal but was a proposal of the whole committee. I am not at all sure that, when the whole story comes to be told, it may not be discovered that, but for the action of the government of Canada in this particular matter, at that particular time, the whole of Europe might have been aflame to-day. What would then have been said of "Canada's proposal"? That is a matter worth considering. I had all this very much in my mind when the other day I was speaking of the appalling consequences of the possible result of words spoken, or action taken, without mature consideration and due authority.
I think I have covered all that I wish to say on that matter at the present time. There is one further subject to which I ought to refer, because it was a promise made by my right hon. friend, and I am afraid it is one that he is apt to overlook. He was critical of the statement I issued on the night of the general elections, October 14, and he said he was going to ask some one of his followers to put this statement on Hansard. I have noticed very often that when my right hon. friend wants to evade a subject and not have it come up again, he states what he is going to do at some other time, and then it is not done. I do not want to have him trouble any of his immediate following, and on the other hand I do not want this statement to go unnoticed; so with his permission and that of the house, I will conclude what I have to say by reading the statement myself. I think it admirably sums up the significance of the recent campaign, and indicates pretty clearly the will and wish and views of the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that the statement I referred to yesterday? Is it the full statement? The statement I had in mind seems rather longer than that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. I know my right hon. friend will regret the length of this statement, but it is the one to .which he referred:
I thank the people of Canada for the confidence they have to-day expressed in Liberal principles and policies, in the Liberal party, and in myself as its leader. The Liberal party has placed its trust in the people. The people to-day have reciprocated that trust in abundant measure. It will not be betrayed.
I congratulate the members of the Liberal party on the splendid campaign they have waged. We have been attacked on all sides, and we have won on all fronts. To-day's overwhelming victory is the response of the people made effective through organized effort in a great cause, which was begun the moment the Liberal party went into opposition in 1930, and which has been carried forward with increasing vigour and determination. In this great effort, men and women, young and old, have equally shared. It has been furthered by a strong and helpful Liberal press; and by efficient organization in all parts of Canada- from the headquarters of the National Liberal Federation in Ottawa and provincial Liberal associations in the provinces, to the committees of Liberal workers in municipalities and in the remotest rural polls.
The whole-hearted cooperation of the Liberal ' premiers and governments of eight of the nine provinces of Canada was an exceptionally significant feature of the campaign, and one which may be expected to contribute in no uncertain way to the solution of many of our country's perplexing problems.
To-day's victory is a victory for democracy. It discloses that the people may be relied upon to exercise their judgment clearly, in spite of innumerable and unscrupulous efforts to divert the electorate from the real issues before them. It constitutes a great deliverance; a deliverance of the people from one-man government, from mistaken policies, and from autocratic leadership. It is a triumph for broad principles and policies, as against promises and pledges recklessly and extravagantly made for the sole purpose of winning an election. It is a declaration that tradition, experience and achievement are still regarded by tbe Canadian people as one of the greatest assets a political party may possess. It is a direct response to the Liberal protest against all forms of dictatorship in Canada, whether they incline towards Fascism, Socialism or Sovietism, and equally against endless and dangerous experimentation in matters of government. It is a direct response to the appeal for the maintenance of British parliamentary practice and procedure. It proclaims the end of tbe superman idea. It is dear evidence of the desire of the people of Canada to maintain high standards in Canadian public life, and to enjoy a tone in the discussion of public affairs wholly different from that to which, both in and out of parliament, they have become accustomed during the last five years. It makes clear that the people of Canada have had enough of "blasting" methods, and of the "iron heel";

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
that they wish to see concord replace discord, and cooperation replace dissension within our own borders; and that good will and not ill will should prevail between Canada and other countries.
The results afford the strongest condemnation of the attempts made by the Bennett government to debauch the people with expenditures from the public treasury, and of the efforts made by Mr. Bennett himself to intimidate the electorate through fear, by raising the bogeys of communism, of the undermining of Canada's industrial standards by unrestricted oriental and other foreign competition, and of the wholesale destruction which he said would await industry under a Liberal government. They afford a conclusive condemnation of the unworthy means employed in the endeavour to effect a so called national government in Canada; to do, after an election, what no political party was prepared to sponsor in the campaign itself. It is proof of the folly of individuals, whatever their motives, summoning new political parties into being, giving them their names and programs, and expecting any appreciable measure of support. It is to be hoped that the campaign of 1935 will witness tile end of hysteria, and a speedy return to sanity, in the discussion and administration of the country's affairs.
In the present campaign, the Liberal party concentrated upon the issues which it considered to be vital to the recovery of our national life, but it by no means restricted its discussion to them. It made its position clear upon all questions of immediate concern. The results of to-day's voting may, therefore, be regarded as an all but unanimous endorsation of the principles and policies set forth.
To-day's election discloses that the people share the view, which the Liberal party has all along maintained, that unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem. It is an endorsation of the Liberal proposal to deal with this question by means of a representative national commission, and by policies which will serve to revive industry and trade.
The results make equally clear that the people generally share the view, kept to the fore by the Liberal party, that trade is the basis of industrial and commercial development; and that a Canadian government should do all in its power to negotiate trade agreements with all countries willing to trade with Canada on a reciprocal basis. The results make clear that the people of Canada are opposed to planning for scarcity by the restriction of production, of trade, and of employment, and that they are not satisfied with the Ottawa trade agreements, and welcome the prospect of their early revision. Everywhere Mr. Bennett has said that the verdict of this election would be a verdict for or against the empire trade pacts of 1932. There can no longer be any mistake as to what the people think of those agreements and of Mr. Bennett's methods of their negotiation.
The election is an unmistakable verdict in favour of the liberation of external and internal trade; and in favour of a reciprocal agreement with the United States, and of the restoration of trade with Japan upon a mutually beneficial basis in the case of each of these countries. It constitutes a demand for the abolition of the extravagant increases in the tariff, together with the removal of arbitrary taxes and
12739-7i
regulations, as imposed by the present administration, which have had the effect of strangling the commerce of the nation, exploiting consumers, and robbing railways of business. It is a demand for an end to the making and altering of tariffs by executive action, and for the substitution of stability for uncertainty in the administration of customs laws. It is an overwhelming condemnation of the policies of economic nationalism, economic isolation, and economic imperialism, upon which the present government has proceeded in all its legislation; and a corresponding demand for the substitution of policies which will make for economic freedom, national expansion, and international good will.
The election is an endorsation of the Liberal view that credit is a public matter, not of interest to bankers only but of direct concern to every citizen. It is a verdict against a privately owned and controlled central bank, and in favour of a properly constituted national bank to perform the functions of rediscount and the control of currency issue considered in terms of public need. There can be no mistaking the demand for a restoration to the government of Canada of control over credit and currency issue. As the campaign proceeded the issue of the control, by the people, of all functions of government, through their representatives in parliament, and not by any other power, became increasingly clear. The electorate has declared that a responsible ministry, not organized finance and international money power, is to control in all matters of state.
The election is an overwhelming verdict against amalgamation of the railways of Canada and against the creation of other monopolies, whether related to the agencies of transportation and communication, production, trade, industry or banking.
It is a verdict for the democratization of industry and the rights of labour and consumers to have their voice heard and influence felt in the control of industrial policy. It is a warning and rebuke to arrogant employers of labour who have sought to intimidate their employees and to prevent them from enjoying the free exercise of the franchise which is the birthright of every Canadian citizen.
Above all, the election is a demand for the restoration of responsible government in Canada, and government not by a single individual but by the collective wisdom of many minds. The people have expressed their determination to end one man government and to reverse the trend of the past five years in the direction of dictatorship. They have overwhelmingly condemned the present government and the abri-trary and autocratic methods by which it has proceeded from the day it assumed office, and the manner in which it has persistently defied the unmistakable will of the people.
It is a verdict in favour of personal liberty, electoral reform, and of measures which will, among other things, prevent the national radio being surreptitiously used by any political party for the defamation of character.
It is a verdict in favour of the reduction of the burden of public debt and taxation, and in favour of the attainment of a balanoed budget.
It is a verdict in favour of those courses in international relations which will make for peace and good will.
It is a verdict in favour of a more equitable distribution of wealth, with increasing regard
