The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
to human need, to the furtherance of social justice, and to the promotion of the common good.
These are all principles and policies which the Liberal party has consistently and continuously espoused, and for which it has steadily fought. We began the fight for these policies and principles in the parliament of Canada. We carried our advocacy of them to the people in byelections and in provincial elections. The voice of the people, though clear and decisive, remained unheeded, and their will and wish ignored. We have now submitted our policies to the people in a general election. We have received their endorsation. We shall proceed to put these policies into effect.
A century ago Liberalism in Canada had its birth in the struggle for political liberty and responsible government. The existence of both has been threatened in the period of time that Mr. Bennett has been at the head of affairs. They have been maintained in the measure they have only by continuous and strenuous effort on the part of Liberals in and out of parliament. They will now be fully restored by a Liberal government.
In the new era which dawns to-day the struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before. Poverty and adversity, want and misery, are the enemies which Liberalism will seek to banish from our land. They have lain in wait at the gate of every Canadian home during the past five years, and their menacing mien has served to destroy the souls as well as the minds and bodies of an ever increasing number of men, women and children in our land. We take up at once, as our supreme task, the endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty, starvation and unnecessary suffering in a land of abundance, discontent and distress in a country more blessed by providence than any other on the face of the globe, and to gain for individual lives, and for the nation as a whole, that "health and peace and sweet content" which is the rightful heritage of all.
The people of Canada have made clear that, in their opinion, "present material interests," and a course of action which does not distinguish between materialistic and spiritual values, must make way for something nobler in the conduct of a nation's affairs; and that self-seeking and selfishness, however much they may appear to lead to worldly success, are not the paths of true greatness either for an individual or a nation. The people of Canada to-day have reaffirmed their faith in the ancient and beneficent precepts that it is only by sharing each other's burdens and doing unto others as we would have others do unto us that men and nations can serve their own best interest and the common good.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite unnecessary for me to attempt to cover the ground gone over by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), nor do I consider it necessary to repeat the formal compliments which have already been given. I might how-

ever express my appreciation of the very kind reference to myself made by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght).
We have heard a good deal in the way of echoes from the last election and the general political situation. I do not intend to spend much time on that sort of thing. It may be inevitable that we should have some crowing by the victors, although I must say that the spectacle is not very edifying. While there may be something in the statement that we have been delivered from a one man government, we might ask whether we have been delivered from minority government. The point made by the leader of the opposition was not, I think, answered by the Prime Minister, the fact being that of all those who were eligible to vote only some thirty-five per cent did vote for the party which now is represented on the government side in such very large numbers.
A lot of persons who were counted as voters were dead and buried.

The fact that such a large number of members were elected by a minority of votes does not really touch the point, because the government, having such a large majority, is able to exercise almost complete control over legislation that may be proposed in this house, and certainly can determine whether or not any legislation shall pass. As a matter of fact, of the total vote cast, 4.392,227, the Liberals received 2,058,699. The plea	used to	be made	that	we	should
have representation by population. I have wondered, in view of .the figures I have just given, whether there should not be some change in the electoral system that would give a larger measure of equity.
I have in my possession a document which is now worn almost thin. It is entitled Liberals and Labour, and was issued by the National Liberal committee in 1921, publication	No 11.	Resolution	No.	10	therein
accepts the principle of proportional representation. I do not know whether that is today a part of Liberal policy. We in our corner every once in. a while for some fifteen years tried to bring that particular resolution of the Liberal party to the attention of the Liberals. For nine years of those fifteen the Liberals were in office, and it does seem to me that if they are true to the principles they enunciated and gave to the public some years ago we should have something in the nature of electoral reform brought down at this session of the house.
The Prime Minister referred to those of us in this section of the house and classed us all

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
together as independents. I would almost have thought he would do us the courtesy of using the names which we have chosen and which have become familiar to the whole country.
It is the new democracy.
Instead of that he rather arrogantly classes us all together as independents. We are not Liberals; we are not Conservatives, we are a strange assortment that has to be put all together.
Thank heaven for that!

I suppose if the Prime Minister chooses to adopt that terminology we shall have to submit, but I suggest that it does not add to the clarity of our discussions or the good will of an assemblage of this kind when one individual, even a prime minister, attempts for his own purposes to class together people who have just come through a campaign in which they have very clearly set out their differences one from the other, and to say that "although I put these all together in one group, it is manifest that these people differ among themselves."
But since we have all been put together I point out that one of the most significant features of the recent election is that over a million people voted for one or another of the groups or individuals that are neither Liberal nor Conservative. I think it is a remarkable thing that a million people in Canada should express dissatisfaction with the old historical parties and with that for which the old historical parties stand. I would remind the government that although they seem to be so firmly entrenched, those wrho are to be classed as independent, the riffraff as it were, do represent over half the number of votes that were cast for the Liberals who are now in the seats of the mighty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend what term he would use in describing the parties other than the official opposition and the government? What term does he suggest? I did not wish to be offensive; I was seeking what I thought would be the most acceptable term in referring collectively to those groups which are other than the official opposition and the government.
If the Prime Minister must refer to them, possibly the phraseology which he himself has just now used might be acceptable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is that?

"Groups other than the official opposition." It may be proper to group together those who are standing on more or less the same platform as the Liberals, but I repeat, it does not add anything to the understanding of our national problems to attempt to put together groups that have very little in common and then to proceed further and say that these groups differ among themselves. I just point that out in passing. My point is that these groups who are so classed together obtained from the electorate half as many votes as those obtained by the Liberals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They do not agree as well as we do.

One of the most humorous slogans of the election in my judgment was this: "Elect King and get action." I wish it were true, because I have been long enough in this house to desire action above almost anything else. I would point out that the government have, as they boast, a very large majority in the house. Further than that, as they again boast, most of the provincial governments are of the same political complexion as themselves. Under these circumstances I would say that the government have absolutely no excuse for lack of action. It is clear that with a large majority in the house and with most of the provinces of the same political complexion the government have absolutely no excuse for non-action. Undoubtedly a large number of people voted for the Liberals in the hope of securing action. Now the Liberals have their chance. We in our small group will do our utmost to cooperate with the government in any sort of progressive legislation. We are small in numbers, but we represent a constituency of nearly 400,000 people. Our attitude in the house in the past has been and will continue to be that of giving support to a government on any progressive legislation, and we wish the present government well in the great task upon which they have entered.
I hold in my hand a leaflet which indicates the Liberal party's position on some immediate problems. It was issued by the National Liberal Federation of Canada, 114 Wellington street, Ottawa, just prior to the election.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Two years
ago.

I suppose the position would be the same to-day as it was two years ago. So far as I can see the leaflet is not dated. Additional copies of the leaflet may be obtained at a cost of

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
thirty-five cents per hundred. As I read the speech from the throne my thoughts were directed to this leaflet. As a matter of fact, in that speech very little progressive legislation is adumbrated-very little. We have a very small legislative program before us. I may be permitted to call attention to several items, the absence of which is very significant.
The leaflet indicates, in the opening paragraph, that the Liberal party considers "unemployment of first concern." In the speech from the throne we find the observation that unemployment is Canada's most urgent problem. That being so, it is unfortunate the Prime Minister had not a word to say concerning unemployment in that short three and a half hour speech of his. As unemployment is one of Canada's outstanding problems, I say it is unfortunate the right hon. gentleman did not say something about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but I must remind him that I did refer to legislation, and also mentioned the amount of employment which had been given as a result of one or two measures for which the government is already responsible.

More employment may have been mentioned, but I believe hon. members will bear me out when I say that no statement was made as to what the government intended to do with regard to the great problem of unemployment. In the leaflet before me the Liberal party had stated that we should have a representative national commission. I believe that is promised in the speech from the throne. They had this further to say, however:
As permanent measures the Liberal party is pledged to introduce policies which will serve to provide employment by reviving industry and trade-
Then I should like to draw attention to the following words appearing in bold type, "And to introduce a national system of unemployment insurance." The government may say that we already have such a system, and that its constitutionality is now being tested before the courts. I am aware of that; but we have no indication from the government as to what it proposes to do or what its attitude may be. We know very well that last year the Liberal party criticized severely indeed the proposals offered by the then government. What are we to expect in the next year or so? What are we to have by way of relief in the meantime? Those

are the matters about which I am concerned. There is no definite proposal put forward by the government in the speech from the throne.
Again we find that this leaflet calls for the "control of investments," and the following paragraph appears in relation thereto:
The Liberal party believes the financial mismanagement of industry is largely responsible for many conditions obtaining to-day.
To prevent exploitation of the public through the sale of watered stocks and worthless securities, it believes an investment control board should be established, with supervision of issues of securities by companies incorporated under federal charters.
I quite agree with the idea behind that statement, but we have no indication in the speech from the throne that anything of the kind is proposed. So far as I know this matter is not before the courts. The constitutionality of a measure of this kind is not in question. Why does not the government propose to implement the statement of policy it gave to the country?
Further than that with regard to the democratization of industry, to which the Prime Minister referred even as late as the date of the leaflet, which was issued on the night of the election, we find this:
The Liberal party believes that industrial reconstruction is the problem of the future. It will seek in industrial relations as opportunity offers to give to workers and consumers a larger share in the government of industry.
So far as I can see there is no indication in the speech from the throne that anything is to be done at this session to implement that promise. I wish something could be done. Meantime many workers are engaged in industries in which they have no chance for anything like freedom. It is not sufficient simply to pass pious resolutions of this kind-I will not say "to make promises," because the Prime Minister is supposed not to have made any promises. I say it is not sufficient to pass resolutions and send out statements of this kind without seeking to implement them at the earliest possible opportunity.
Then, in a reference to the "more equitable distribution of wealth," we find this paragraph:
The Liberal party recognizes that the problem of distribution has become more important than that of production, and believes that personality is more sacred than property. It will devote itself to finding ways and means of effecting a fair and just distribution of wealth with increasing regard to human need, to the furtherance of social justice and to the promotion of the common good.
Those are fine sounding phrases with which we may all agree. But I must ask this: What indication is there in the speech from the

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
throne that at this session any legislation will be brought down to carry out the statements contained in the leaflet?
Under the circumstances I should like to propose an amendment to the address in reply, seconded by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that the following words be added to the motion:
"We respectfully regret, however, that Your Excellency's present advisers have not indicated that they have any policy or intend to take definite and immediate steps to end the prevailing poverty and insecurity of the masses by making available to the people of Canada the great actual and potential wealth of the country."
I think all hon. members have recognized the serious nature of the depression through which we have 'been passing. I, for one, sympathize with any government called upon to administer capitalism under these conditions. Frankly, however, what I am afraid of is that with the slightest move toward an upswing in conditions, the government will refuse to take that radical action so essential under existing circumstances. On every side we are hearing talk about returning prosperity, and I suppose if some slight betterment in conditions comes to us there is no doubt that the government will take credit for having brought this about. That of course is the ordinary practice of politicians. I would say this, however, that as I analyze the situation, and as we have been trying in past years to place the case before parliament, I cannot believe we are going to have any permanent prosperity, and I am suggesting it is time to give attention to some of the more radical policies which we believe to be necessary. In the first place, we face a greatly increased productive capacity. In his book on Technics and Civilization, Mr. Lewis Mumford states that the average workman to-day has the equivalent of 240 mechanical slaves, and can do in a week what would need four years and seven months to do unaided. If the ordinary working man is capable with machinery of producing such a great quantity of wealth or new material, what are we going to do with the workmen who "are not .needed? Undoubtedly that is one of the main problems that face us at the present time. I do hope that in this house we shall not begin once more to say that either one government or the other is responsible for unemployment. Undoubtedly unemployment is due to grave economic maladjustments. The question is: How is any government going to solve this problem?
The federal reserve board in the United States recently reported:
In February last industrial production was 90 per cent of the 1923-1925 averse, but the employment was only 80 per cent and payrolls only 64 per cent.
I fancy that conditions obtaining in Canada are very similar. What do those figures mean? They mean that production is up; that employment is lagging, and that payrolls are lagging still more. That is a serious situation from the strictly economic standpoint. Let me repeat: It means that production is up; employment is lagging, but payrolls are lagging still more.
The United States government has appropriated some twelve million dollars to make surveys into the trends of employment and production. Some of the facts which instigated the inquiry were these: From 1919 to 1929 volume of production in manufacturing industries increased 37 per cent, while employment dropped 2 per cent. Freight car loadings increased 6 per cent from 1923 to 1929, and employment on steam railways declined 10 per cent.
I will just interject that they have no Canadian National railway problem there, and that is one of the reasons I am using these American figures. Further, according to the statement before me, coal production increased 10 per cent from 1919 to 1929, while employment dropped 14 per cent. Despite an increase in production of agricultural commodities, 800,000 agricultural workers were displaced between 1919 and 1927. That the trend shown by the data given above has continued since 1929 is indicated by the fact that the output per man hour in manufacturing industries is estimated to have increased approximately 25 per cent between 1929 and 1935.
You see the seriousness of those statistics. In commenting on a similar situation in Great Britain, W. G. Gray, president of the British Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, says:
We are face to face with something entirely new in human experience.
My quarrel with Liberal doctrine is not that it advocates individual freedom and all that kind of thing, but rather that Liberal policies are essentially based on conditions that no longer exist. If we are to secure true individual freedom and true security we shall have to recognize the conditions that are here now and that are apparently permanent.
I should like to call the attention of the house, and particularly those members who do not read the New Republic regularly, to a very illuminating article by Mr. Chase which appeared in its issue of December 18, 1935. Mr. Chase admits that business is more active; that profit levels have improved; that the dollar volume of retail sales is substan-

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
tially a'boye what it was a year ago; that the annual income is increasing; that power output and machine-tool production are back to 1929 levels, indicating among other things an augmented flow of labour-saving devices with inanimate energy to power them; that new motor cars, most of them bought on the instalment plan, are filling the roads; that the stock market is becoming active.
Then he gives the other side of .the picture: Car loadings tend to remain on the same plateau; unemployment remains; construction industry is still a third less than normal; commercial loans are declining.
Then he puts his finger upon the real difficulty. He says:
Commercial loans are falling; government loans are rising.
It is curious .that in the bank statements which appear in our papers that particular fact has not received very much emphasis. Commercial loans are falling; government loans are rising. Mr. Chase goes on to say:
The whole balance rests not on a regained equilibrium in private enterprise, after a purging of capital claims, but on government credit. The private-capital market is not functioning, as it did in the upswing from all earlier depressions. Meanwhile, billions of capital claims have not been squeezed' out. Outgo is padded with huge "unnatural" capital charges. The principal, including common stocks, of capital claims is still in the neighbourhood' of three hundred billions, and a return is demanded as heretofore. Government debts are rapidly being added to the total. The amount of savings that must be promptly and frequently reallocated to preserve balance is enormous.
Then a little bit further on he makes this very significant statement which I confess I had not considered before reading his article. He says:
"Balance the budget," cries the sound money camp, but to balance the government budget to-day can only mean to unbalance the dollar system.
I think that is a very, very important consideration. On every side people are urging the government to balance the budget, but I would venture to say that if the government does balance its budget the very people who are now urging this would be the first to be seriously affected because to do so would unbalance the whole financial system, for today an important sphere of investment is government bonds.
I see it is almost six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to emphasize that whatever party may be in power, it must face an economic situation that is unprecedented, and any prosperity that may come to us, if my an-

alysis is at all correct, is bound to be of the most temporary character. We must build for the future.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

When the house rose I was endeavouring to point out some of the prominent economic trends which prevail to-day and which we must recognize if we would solve the problems that confront us. I pointed out that while production was going up, wages were not going up correspondingly, and that employment also was lagging behind. There are important consequences which of necessity follow from that situation. In the very first place we face the lack of consuming power; unless wages are paid we cannot hope that the goods which are produced will be bought. That is one of our fundamental troubles today, and under the capitalist system if goods are not bought there is a slackening of the machinery of production. People will not produce unless profits can be obtained, and the slackening of production, following a vicious circle, leads to a still greater. measure of unemployment and still lower wages.
Further, there is one other economic result that is all important from the standpoint of the system itself; we reach a point where, if profits cannot be obtained, the system stalls. I think we are now very near that position. As I said once in the house Last year, when I read some socialist economists many years ago I used to wonder exactly what was meant by the contradictions of capitalism. To-day, I believe, we understand only too well because we live in an era in which these contradictions are 'becoming apparent to us all.
Another of these trends about which I should like to speak is this, that expanding markets are not readily available and certainly cannot 'be depended upon to solve our economic problems. Five years ago when we assembled in this house the Conservatives stressed the possibility of unemployment being solved by higher tariffs. The years since then have demonstrated that their solution did not work. The Liberals now come into office and they emphasize the possibility of wider markets. I am quite confident that the next five years, and perhaps a much shorter period than that, will demonstrate that their scheme will not work either. The trouble is deeper than the question of protection or of lower tariffs.

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
I was very much interested in reading in the Manitoba Free Press of January 11, 1936, a letter from Miss E. Cora Hind, who, as everyone knows, is quite a specialist on agricultural affairs. Miss Hind writes:
Having now visited Norway, Sweden, Germany, Poland, Roumania, Jugoslavia, Hungary, Austria and Czechoslovakia, and looked into the possibility of these countries for the export of Canadian wheat, I must frankly confess that I am disappointed at the outlook. Before leaving Canada, I in common with many others felt that a change in government, and more liberal customs and trade arrangements, would be practically all that was needed to reestablish much of the former trade to Europe. I feel now that the task, while not an impossible one, will be a more difficult one and will take more time than was anticipated.
Commenting on this editorially, the Free Press said:
Miss Hind's judgment on this point, based as it is on personal investigation, will be accepted as authoritative.
The latter .part of the editorial is less ingenuous when it suggests that it is easier to throw markets away than to whistle them back. It is not going to be easy to find markets for our wheat, and I suggest that it is not going to be easy to-day to find markets for any large export from Canada. I do not want to go into an argument which I have used previously in .this house, but I would point out that in the earlier days of capitalism there was nearly always an expanding market. It was in those days that the trade of Great Britain flourished. Later on other nations came into the picture. They too began to export to countries that had once been consumer countries and had become themselves producer countries and thus competitors of Great Britain. Since the war that tendency has greatly increased. We witness perhaps the outstanding example in Japan, which a few years ago used to consume our goods but is now producing and exporting not merely consumable goods but capital goods as well.
I do not think the Liberal doctrine has sufficiently recognized the development which has taken place in the capitalist system. The Liberal party is still depending upon a constantly enlarged market to keep the system going and to bring back prosperity. I do not say that there cannot be developed or found certain markets; I hope there will be. But I do say that we cannot depend upon a constantly increasing market as an economic solution of our problems.
A change of government has taken place, but I submit that our pressing problems remain unchanged. Among these I would call special attention to the unemployment situation and the distress that prevails at the present time. According to a statement made ' about a month ago by the Canadian Welfare Association, while employment in Canada has reached its highest level since December, 1930 relief costs have not moved correspondingly downward, and there are still more than one million Canadians in receipt of direct unemployment relief. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is not in his place, but undoubtedly he can give us the very latest figures. I fancy, however, that the figures I have just given are substantially correct. Take my own city. In Winnipeg nearly 24.000 heads of families have registered since 1924. In 1933, the peak was 9.734 families and in September, 1935, it was 7,309.
I need not speak of the demoralizing effect of this situation upon families that for some years have been on relief. In the first place these families are being crowded into very narrow and inadequate living quarters. The whole standard of living is 'being lowered; for whereas a few years ago it was considered necessary, for a moderately sized family, that there should be at least three or four rooms, to-day the ordinary family is being housed in two rooms. This surely is not sufficient to maintain what we have regarded as a Canadian standard of living. And that is not in a few individual cases; it is a wholesale matter. Food, perhaps, is more or less adequate. but there are a great many things besides meat and potatoes that people need in order to have a proper variety in their food; and as regards extras of any kind, the people are very greatly lacking. Household supplies have run down during these years, and we are faced with a serious state of affairs throughout the country.
In rural Manitoba the director of public health nurses recently asked for clothing for 600 children who otherwise would not continue a.t school during the winter. The Junior League, which is not at all a radical organization, in offering assistance stated' its belief that the responsibility for providing clothing for destitute children is a necessary government service and not one for private charity. I quite agree that it is a necessary government service to provide clothing for these 600 children. Think of it! In the small province of Manitoba there are 600 children who, unless they are provided for by charity, cannot go to public school. Surely that is a serious thing in this rich country of ours. I agree that this is a public responsibility, but behind that it is decidedly a public responsibility, a government responsibility, to

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
see that such gifts of charity should noit be ' required; that the need for them should not continue.
I would like to commend the government for its dealing so far with the system of the single men's unemployed camps. I think the evidence which has been brought forward in connection with the reports and investigations that have been made justifies what we said in this corner last year. I am glad to learn that we are to have these camps transferred from the Department of National Defence to the Labour department. This is a good move. We stated here that the difficulty was not primarily that of food, although evidence before the British Columbia commission showed that at that time there was very much to be desired in the way of the food; the real difficulty has been that of segregating large numbers of young people, who ought to be at regular work, who ought to be filled with hope, in these camps where they have remained year after year without any hope of anything better in the future. We have urged, and I would urge again-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
Moved by Mr. Woodsworth, seconded by Mr. Coldwell:
That the following words be added to the motion:
"We respectfully regret, however, that Your Excellency's present advisers have not indicated that they have any policy or intend to take definite and immediate steps to end the prevailing poverty and insecurity of the masses by making available to the people of Canada the great actual and potential wealth of the country."

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the kindness of the Prime Minister in regularizing the action in this way. I would point out that since the Speaker had the motion in his own hand he might at least have read it before the forty minutes had elapsed. I was trying to point out that what was desirable in connection with the young men who are unemployed was real work and real wages. We shall have to wait until the legislation is before us to know just how far the government is prepared to act in this regard. I should like however to say now that, while there is so much work to be done in this country in the way of building and reforestation and so on, there is no reason whatever why the men cannot be given real work that will be of permanent value to this country. Further than that, since these young men are out of work through no fault of their own, there is no reason why the state should not pay them reasonable wages. I was rather sorry to find in the report that a good deal of stress was laid upon the danger of agitators in the camps. There may be agitators in the camps, but I think we all recognize that agitation does not get very far unless there is some ground for agitation. If conditions are not good, as long as men are not slaves they have a right to proclaim the evils that exist or to band themselves together in order to obtain redress from those evils. This was
extremely difficult to do under conditions that prevailed during the last two or three years.
I should like to impress upon the house the necessity of our looking at these unemployed in an altogether different way from what we have been accustomed to do in the past. We have been too much inclined to think that they were near criminals, or that they should be treated as paupers. To-day tens of thousands of people are out of work through no fault of their own. If there is any fault, it is that of the governments of this country that have not been able so to adjust conditions that these men and women could find the work that formerly they had. They should not be penalized more than any other section of the community. They should not be regarded as paupers. There were some men who ran in this election, formerly members of this house, who were defeated. What happened to them? They were provided with jobs of various kinds. Some were found positions in the Senate; some were put on important commissions, and so on. There were other men who belong to the smaller parties in this house who were also defeated. To-day some of them are in the bread line. There is no fundamental difference between the man who is provided with a job in the Senate or on a commission, simply in order that he may be cared for, and the man who is in a relief camp simply because the state has not afforded any way by which he can earn an honest living. We need to get away from the idea that these unemployed people are either paupers or criminals.
There is another matter to which I should like to direct attention, and that is the huge debt which is hanging over our people. I am afraid the hysterical people of this country are not to be found only among the unemployed. I was interested to note this language in a recent issue of the Montreal Daily Star of February 6, 1936:
-this country is on the verge of disaster, nearer to a smash than it has ever been, nearer than it was in 1929, when the economic world rocked about our ears and it seemed as if we were plunging directly into the maelstrom.
And again:
The simple truth in that we are face to face with a crash which, unless it is averted, will blast this country's future and lead us into an economic darkness of such density and duration as to stagger the imagination.
Those are not my words. Possibly some of us will be rather reminded of the "whispers of death" of some years ago. However the facts are serious enough, and I am glad to note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning)

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
nods his head in approval. We have sometimes urged that sooner or later debts will have to be scaled down or the interest will have to be reduced and sometimes we have been told that this means repudiation in whole or in part. I do not like the word "repudiation," but I do say very definitely that just as international debts in practice have been repudiated, so I think it is only a matter
of time until, whether under a Liberal or a Conservative government, these internal debts of ours will have to be materially scaled down. I do not see any other way out. Compulsory conversion is, in effect, a capital levy; it is a form of conscription. "Capital" is surely sufficiently alert to its own interests to be willing to surrender a little to save a great ' deal. We have never succeeded in distributing the sacrifice of war evenly among our people

I am delighted indeed to find a commercial organization taking that ground, which I may say we have taken again and again.

Listen:
-there seems no good reason why people of means should be less willing, in emergency, to surrender a portion of their wealth than they would their own or their sons' bodies. Internal disruption is not less dangerous than foreign aggression whether we think in terms of liberty, social institutions or trade. If compulsory conversion is 'to be avoided, self interest may dictate what patriotism merely urges.
I commend that to business men in this country. I think it is rather important, and I delight to have it come from at least a few of the people who are recognized in the business world. Let me read it again:
If compulsory conversion is to be avoided, self interest may dictate what patriotism merely urges.
I take it that the time is coming when we shall have to consider very carefully the

burdens that rest upon the people of this country.
There are very serious conditions indeed among the farmers of the west. Last year for some weeks I was out among the farmers in southwestern Manitoba and southern Saskatchewan where I found the most deplorable conditions, due not to unemployment but very largely to climatic conditions coupled with the enormous debts which the farmers have to carry. I met families whom I had known thirty years ago, when they were in a fair way to success; to-day they are living on relief, and whole communities are desperate. I found some families who had moved to northern Saskatchewan-and there are members from that district who know these conditions as well as or better than I do-living in a destitute condition. What have we done for these people? We have handed them out a little bit of relief. It is quite true that some provision was made by this house some years ago for dealing with the drought situation. I believe a few ponds have been dug for the storage of water.; I believe here, there and yonder a little has been done in the way of strip farming, but nothing has been done on a very extensive scale and certainly no adequate provisions has been made that would allow these farmers to maintain their standards of living and their self respect. I ask why these conditions should be perpetuated at a time when other people are living in comparative luxury. There is no reason whatever for such a situation.
Since taking office the government has been active along several lines. To-day we heard about the United States agreement. Personally I think it is good as far as it goes, but I should like to ask: What about the method employed? We are told it is an agree-

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
ment rather than a treaty, and as such most of its clauses do not need to be ratified by parliament. That is the information we have been given. I am inclined to think that if the Prime Minister, were sitting on this side of the house he would have a great deal to say about such an action taking away the rights of parliament. Some hon. members may recall what he said several years ago in connection with the Ottawa conference. In discussing the agreements there made he said, according to Hansard for 1932-1933, volume I, at page 41, in urging that the government should have made only a tentative agreement:
We are no longer free to settle in our own parliament what our fiscal policy is to be because that has been settled for us by a meeting of the executives of different parts of the empire, and that without consultation with their several parliaments in advance.... Will this House of Commons have the right to alter one line of those agreements? Will this house have any opportunity of lowering or raising any duties as fixed in those agreements? Will the British government have that right? On the contrary, will not all legislative bodies be told, "These agreements were arrived at in the conference at Ottawa and they are to be put through without any change whatever." What then becomes of the freedom of parliament? What is the significance of parliament in that event? Why have a parliament at all, if executives of different parts of the empire can meet together and lay down a new imperial policy and compel its adoption by the imputation of a want of patriotism or a desire to bring about the dismemberment of the empire, as against those who are not prepared to support such measures?
Well, I personally do not worry a great deal about the method, but I should like the Prime Minister at his leisure to explain why it is that he complains so bitterly of the methods used at the Imperial conference in regard to the Ottawa agreements and yet feels free to bring to this house an agreement which need not be ratified in its details by the house, but which, we are told, is to go through as arranged.

speechtext: I do not like to interrupt, but the two are entirely different. May I say that all that has been effected up to the present has been the reduction of certain duties under a statute that this parliament passed, which gave to the government authority to reduce duties at any time provided a like concession was made to it by some other country. The agreement to which I took exception and to which my hon. friend has referred was an agreement which increased duties, put additional taxation on the people of this country without parliament having authorized anything of the kind by statute or otherwise.

Well, we may leave that to be threshed out in future. Personally I cannot see wherein the difference lies. I am glad it is in the direction of lower tariffs, but at the same time I do not see that the method in the two cases is so fundamentally different.
Then there is the question of Japan. The other day I read an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press, a paper which I try to read from time to time, in which the statement was made that the duty had been reduced from 176 per cent to 148 per cent. I am not sure whether that is true. The Free Press commented at that time that this was under a Liberal government; that the manufacturers of the east should not make a great fuss when they still have a protection of 148 per cent. There is, I believe, some question as to the rate, but I understand that in any event it is over 100 per cent. I should like to call this to the attention of my friend the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Deachman) and ask whether he is altogether satisfied that under a Liberal government we should still have a duty of 100 per cent.
However I do rejoice to-night in the partial conversion of the Liberals. I congratulate them on calling the bluff of the textile people. I recall several years ago an excellent statement made by the hon. member for Beau-ha rnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond), as to the enormous profits made by the corporation concerned. I think the Free Press in its editorial had a note that during the five years 1930-1934 the Dominion Textiles Company had distributed dividends amounting to $7,091,000, at the same time paying low wages. Undoubtedly the government has done well in calling the bluff of that corporation. But there is one further point. The Liberals are actually recognizing the need for state intervention. They are not as hopeless as I thought. I hope that in the future the precedent which they have adopted in this case will be carried out.
There is one other proposal in the speech from the throne to which I wish to refer, and that is tihe national loan board. Perhaps something of this kind is inevitable. But it is indeed an irony that it should be a Liberal government which proposes that the provinces should surrender their autonomy in financial affairs. If such action is taken there
no

The Address-Mr. Woodsworlh
should be an assumption by the dominion government of a corresponding responsibility for social services. It is curious how we are quite willing to centralize the mounted police force, but not willing to centralize the giving of relief, the lack of which so largely accounts for the necessity of the mounted police, if indeed there is such necessity. The matter of unemployment is still considered primarily one for the provinces; old age pensions are still considered primarily a provincial matter, as well as health, education, and all those things. Yet now, without taking over any responsibility for these important functions, we are to have centralization in the realm of finance. It seems to me that is very serious indeed. As I thought of this I was reminded of an old Hebrew law, and I turned up the book of Deuteronomy, the fifteenth chapter, and I should like to read, in the revised version, verses 1 and 2; 12 to 14; and 16 and 17:
At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release. And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor shall release that which he hath lent unto his neighbour; he shall not exact it of his neighbour and his brother; because the Lord's release hath been proclaimed ___
If thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee. And when thou lettest him go free from thee, thou shalt not let him go empty; thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy threshing-floor, and out of thy winepress; as the Lord thy God hath blessed thee thou shalt give unto him....
And it shall be, if he say unto thee, I will not go out from thee; because he loveth thee and thine house, because he is well with thee; then thou shalt take an awl, and thrust it through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant forever. And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise.
Well, I suggest that the awl that makes people perpetual slaves may very well prove to be the national loan board. In all seriousness, there is a very great danger that we may stabilize our debts and by so doing place an impossible burden upon the great mass of our people.
In the resolution which I proposed I urged that there is nothing in the speech from the throne that would indicate that any definite or any immediate steps are being taken to relieve the poverty or insecurity of the masses by making available to the people of Canada the great actual and potential wealth of the country. Undoubtedly we have in this country great actual wealth, and we have still greater potential wealth. But the fact is that we have not done anything very definite in distributing this wealth. I do not think I can do better than follow the Prime Minister's example by reading a portion of a speech that I made on a previous occasion. About a year ago, on March 28, 1935, I spoke on the distribution of wealth as follows:
Recently I had occasion to make a study, with the help of some friends, of some of the statistical information supplied by the Year Book and from the census. If the income tax returns are combined with the figures of earnings it is possible to show the distribution of income among a very large section of the population. I may say that we were not able to secure any information as to the distribution of farm incomes. But leaving out farm income, we have some 2,713,000 wage earners and other income receivers for whom it is possible to estimate the distribution of income for the year 1930-31.
Those were the better years.
I have before me a table which gives the distribution of the number of income receivers, other than agricultural, and their income in Canada, for the year 1930-31. This is a short table, and with the permission of the house I will place it on Hansard in its present form.

The other 20 per cent of the income receivers, those getting more than $1,500 per year, secured almost half of the total income.
