According to this statement, the great majority of the income receivers, that is,
1,526,000,	receive less than $1,000 per year. I would point out that the family budget as published by the Dominion Department of Labour provides for $800 for food and housing for a family. On that basis a family would need an annual income of from $i,200 to $1,500 to meet the requirements for a decent standard of living, but according to the statistics of the government the vast majority of the people of this country are forced to live on a standard below what would be considered as reasonable. There is no need for such things in a country like this possessing such great resources and spendlid equipment.
On that occasion I went on to refer to a committee appointed a year and a half ago, I believe by the federal government of the United States, to consider what it was possible to produce in that country, with their present equipment, if the equipment were properly organized. The figure established was $4,400 per family. That is. without any additions to their present industrial equipment, and using what they have to full capacity, it would be possible to produce in the United States an income of $4,400 per family. I fancy that the conditions in that country are not greatly dissimilar from those in Canada. We will put the figure at $4,000, if you like, or even at $3,000. In contrast, the vast majority of families in Canada are receiving less than $1,000, a great many in the vicinity of $600 or $700, and many more are out of work and hence are receiving no regular income, only that derived from state or charity.
That is a serious condition. Are we not stupid if we continue a system whereby most of the people are receiving less than $1,000, when it is possible for us to double, treble or quadruple that amount? I put that before the government. We go along year after year after year, following the same old lines. I do urge sincerely that the members of this house very definitely insist that we seriously consider what can be done towards providing for the needs of the masses of the people of Canada. Everyone admits that we have great wealth; everyone admits that we have still greater potential wealth. We cannot see how we can let the government pass this address without urging our point of view, and stating
that in failing to make some more definite provision for the needs of the masses the government is failing to perform its real task.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations concerning the speech from the throne. Last night the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) indicated that he wlas in some doubt as to the stand which a number of hon. members in this section of the chamber were going to take with respect to the support of his government. I shall deal briefly with that point.
In a general way we feel that the speech from the throne is not quite full enough; that it does not go far enough and is not exact enough in the treatment which i,t prescribes for the grievous ills afflicting our country to-day. There is, however, one section of the speech from the throne which appeals to us strongly. Taken along with other pronouncements which have been made on the subject by the Prime Minister we feel that possibly this is sufficiently definite. We desire to be exceedingly definite about this particular part of the speech from the throne, namely, that part which appears as follows:
The control of credit, and the issue of currency, being public matters of direct concern to every citizen, it is intended, at the present session, to ask parliament to make such changes in the ownership and control of the Bank of Canada, as may be necessary to give to the government a predominant interest in the ownership as well as effective control of the bank.
As we see it, if the Prime Minister and his cabinet intend to do the things we believe they intend to do, they will be taking a step which will require a great deal of courage on their part, because they will be doing something which has long been necessary and something which will be almost revolutionary. In their steps forward to this momentous reform they will find the social credit people solidly behind them at every step.
First of all, however, may I refer to some of the things we assume they mean by this statement. We want to make sure that it is going far enough, and that it would constitute a real solution of the difficulties confronting us as a people. May I read one or two further passages which we place alongside the statement in the speech from the throne? First I shall refer to some observations of the Prime Minister delivered on the evening of October 14, a speech which has caused me greatly to admire the right hon. gentleman. I cannot remember a time when a man has made an election promise so quickly after his

The Address-Mr. Blackmore

I do not wish to occupy your attention longer, Mr. Speaker, on this point, though there are a great many other passages I might quote. With your permission, however, I would refer to some figures published by R. J. Scrutton in the April, 1935, number of the magazine Prosperity. He is using round numbers, quoting the American Bureau of Economic Research. He says that in the United States, in a given year, $60,000,000,000 worth of consumable goods, food, clothing, shelter and the like was produced by their industry, but that in that year, when they counted up all the money which was distributed in the United States in the form of wages, dividends, salaries, commissions, and in every other conceivable way in which men could get money with which to buy, there was only $45,000,000,000, and when you discounted $5,000,000,000, which was put into life insurance and thus taken away from the stream which could be used to buy goods, there was only $40,000,000,000. In other words, in the United States in that year there was $20,000,000,000 worth of goods which the American people did not have purchasing power to buy.
What would the United States do with that $20,000,000,000 worth of goods? The figures represent the condition, more or less extreme, which exists in every civilized and industrialized nation at the present time. If the United States undertakes to trade off this $20,000,000,000 worth of goods, receiving $20,000,000,000 worth of French goods, say, in exchange, how can the people of the United States buy that quantity of French goods when they were unable to buy their own? Here we see the secret of the difficulty in international trade.
Now the trouble is purely one of finance. As an indication of this may I quote an authority. Sir Basil Blackett, director of the Bank of England, has made this statement:
When I think of what we have done with money, and what money has done to us, I think we are all fit for a lunatic asylum.
Again let me quote Lord Melchett, the former Sir Alfred Mond, director of Barclay's Bank, of Imperial Chemical Industries, of the International Nickel Company of Canada, and so on:
The world' gets 3 per cent richer every year. This gradual increase of the world's wealth is due mainly to the discoveries of science and the development of industry. We must learn the economies of plenty and forget the economies of scarcity. In the near future our currency and our economics will have to be based on quite different ideas from the past.
Now what are the things upon which our currency is to be based? That is the question, and I leave that for us all to consider. I

have here another quotation which probably will be of interest. At the annual meeting of the Canadian Bank of Commerce of January, 1935, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of January 15, 1935, Sir John Aird, president, stated:
No one now realizes more clearly than our legislators that the cost of public services is out of proportion to the population and its income. The situation cannot be relieved by increased borrowing, or by shifting part of the burden of the care of unemployed people from one legislative group to another. It is now quite generally agreed that continuous borrowing to cover deficits and to maintain social services on the present scale cannot go on indefinitely.
We must find, therefore, as a nation, some other way of getting money. The unemployment problem is increasing. The need of increasing power in order to enable our people to sell their goods both at home and abroad is growing more and more, and to solve the problem we need money. Our debt interest must be paid, and in order to do this we must have money. We cannot get money from the old sources, because even though we in Canada can produce tremendously we cannot sell and we are obliged to decrease production to keep up the price. How then shall we ever produce enough goods to get ourselves out of debt, to take care of our unemployed and to furnish purchasing power to buy our goods? The problem is staggering and beyond answer unless we find some other source of getting money.
Now what we assume the government means is that it is going to take control of the credit issue in this country in such a way as to do what the bankers have been doing for many years. The bankers have been manufacturing money without any cost to themselves, except perhaps clerical costs. Let me quote a few eminent authorities in this regard. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), the former Secretary of State, in an address before the Canadian Club of Toronto on November 13, 1933, is reported to have said:
The cheque system which has been developed enables the banks to create money without the issue of their printed notes-to create credit money at will for many hundreds of millions of dollars in excess of their note issue.

That certainly does not bear out the statement of the hon. gentleman. Everybody knows that a bank may create credit money under certain conditions. That is admitted everywhere. But they do not create without cost or without undertaking liabilities to the same extent that credit money is created.

The Address-Mr. Pelletier

I submit that all that is perfectly true. At the same time, what banks can so generously do, and lend the proceeds to the government, and charge them good stiff interest for, I submit that governments ought to be able to find some way or another of doing for themselves. Here is another example. Mr. A. de V. Leigh, Secretary of the London Chamber of Commerce, in a statement reprinted in the Ottawa Citizen on June 8, 1934, makes the following statement:
The war was paid for as to 30 per cent by actual money belonging to the people-[DOT]
Is there any one who can see any reason why, then, the people of Great Britain should be taxed almost to death to pay for that war, when they already have paid for it?
-earned by the people; which was invested by the people in war loans; 

Then1 note particularly these words:
-and 70 per cent of the total cost of the war wTas paid for by the banks very kindly making these book entries, costing them nothing except the ink, paper and the time of the clerk, and lending the result to the nation at interest. The nation owes them money in exchange for their promises-to-pay money which they have not got. Further we have been paying them interest on these promises-to-pay ever since. Interest on war loans amounts to something like five million dollars a day.
Now if the government is going to assert complete freedom for the Dominion of Canada, it is going to take control of such issue. It must be safeguarded, we will grant. It must be managed by men who are responsible and who are trained, men who will honestly and successfully manage that aspect of the nation's life in the interests of the people and not in the interests of any private group.
There is one more thing which must be very carefully considered, and we assume that the Prime Minister has this in mind. Up to the present time the backing for money has been gold. Men have got to the point where they virtually worship the gold standard. It is like a golden calf which they worship to their ruin, but the time must come when we will all realize that the backing of money is not necessarily gold. May I read here a statement by an eminent authority which none will presume to question, the Midland Bank, England, the largest bank in the world? Here is an extract from its monthly review, June-July, 1935.
In the past four years the progress of ideas has been rapid-the gold value of sterling has dwindled by forty per cent-neither the government nor the bank does anything about it, and no one is in the slightest degree disturbed, since the pound buys just as much goods and services as in 1931.
In other words, the gold standard has been gradually displaced in England as a backing for goods and services. In our country, with new machinery and scientific knowledge, a high degree of technical skill, and good organization, we can produce an almost infinite amount of goods; and we have hundreds of thousands of men in the country ready to render services; so there ought to be virtually an unlimited backing for what money wish to produce; at least there should be enough backing to give us the money we need.
Stability of the value of the pound in terms of goods has replaced stability in terms of gold.-At the heart of the matter is a change in the official conception of stability-internal stability is bringing us far greater benefits, in solid economic welfare, than the pursuit of fixity of exchange could conceivably yield.-* Clearly this change is nothing short of a revolution,-it indicates an almost complete transformation of the monetary system.
The social credit group in this parliament believes that the Prime Minister favours the introduction of such a revolutionary change: First, that the dominion government will take control of the issue so as to manage it for the people's welfare; and, second, that little by little in so far as it is necessary they will gradually depart from the gold standard and substitute a goods and services backing; and that such other measures will be taken as will tend to the well-being and increase of the wealth of this country. I beg to assure the Prime Minister that if they step forward toward that goal they will find, as I declared a few minutes ago, the social credit group one hundred per cent solidly behind them in all their battles for this end.
Mr. RENE-ANTOINE PELLETIER (Peace River) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty to begin the few remarks which I desire to express this evening in my mother tongue, in order to assert the rights of the race from which I have sprung and in which I take much pride. It, moreover, affords me pleasure to note that the youngest member on the government side-who so eloquently seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne-also belongs to this same race. As numerous French Canadians reside in the constituency which I represent, I equally thought it proper, out of courtesy to them, that my first words in this house should be expressed in the French language.
Being the youngest member of this house, I have been all ears since I have come here, and you may be sure I have taken in everything that has been going on.

Good.
The Address-Mr. Pelletier

One hon. gentleman
says, "Good." Possibly I did not find as much good as I expected I would find. One thing I have noticed particularly is this: The two leaders of the great political parties in Canada have spent several days now throwing at each other flowers which were not always very fresh. I am not the only new member here; there are quite a number of us; and I hope that conditions will be rectified and that in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole we will get down to business and do something that is really serious.
There is something more that I remarked which I cannot let go by without bringing it to the attention of this house. I am not going to take the chance of making statements without referring to Hansard, because I notice that if you do that here, people get quite angry about it. So, Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat here-from Hansard, be it understood-a few words which our leader said the other day when he was expressing sympathy at the death of our king. These are the words:
Mr. Speaker, it has been a great delight to me to hear the expressions of loyal devotion to our king and queen. I should like to add to those expressions just a few words on behalf of the people whom I represent, the loyal social credit people throughout the Dominion of Canada.
It grieved me very deeply to hear some people sniggering and laughing when the words "social credit" were mentioned at that particular time. Our leader had it in mind to express sympathy with our great king who is now gone, and I do not believe that laughter was in the proper place.
There is not very much I can say this evening in regard to the speech from the throne, first of all because my leader has very ably set forth the things we hope to do in this house. The legislative program has yet to come before us, and it is diflicult intelligently to criticize anything before it is brought down in the house. We know, for example, that the government intend to bring in certain measures, but until those measures are brought in it is difficult to say very much about them.
There is one thing, however, to which I should like to refer. That is the paragraph in the speech from the throne dealing with unemployment, in which it is stated that the Liberal party recognize the fact that unemployment is one of the gravest problems in Canada to-day and, that being so, it is their intention to set up a commission in order to find a satisfactory means of dealing with what they call an emergent condition. I hope this

commission will do its work in a very short time; that it will not be one of those commissions that drag on endlessly, digging out a fact here and a fact there. I hope the results will be made known as soon as possible so that we may be able in some measure to better the condition of the people of Canada with the least delay.
We have heard a great deal about the trade agreement between the United States and Canada. We find some people not in accord with lower tariffs; on the other hand we find other people who are not in accord with higher tariffs, but I cannot see the use of either blasting or bargaining our way into the markets of the world if we are to starve at home. It seems to me that the very first thing to do is to seek out the markets that we have, and the most immediate and most convenient one is the home market. I should like to take some hon. members with me to some parts of my constituency; I am sure they would agree that there is a market for clothing and other necessities there; I see it myself, and other people have remarked upon that fact. We have a market in Canada. It is not necessary to seek for a market; all we need do is look after our own Canadian people.
I should like to say a word with regard to Doctor Riddell and the possibility of a war. We find the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) making an address not very long ago, last Saturday evening to be exact, and saying:
"In this connection," said the defence minister, "I want to leave with you the profound thought that you will never have in the Dominion of Canada an adequate system of defence until you create a national sentiment in favour of such a system."
Does this mean that we in Canada are to be taught to uphold the sentiment of warfare and that we must be forever ready to take up arms, or is there some other meaning attached to that statement? This is significant at this time, when the question of Doctor Riddell's action is under consideration. According to the orders of the day it is the intention of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) to ask the government to supply him with the correspondence exchanged between the government of Canada and Doctor Riddell. Now we find the Minister of Justice making a statement to the effect that we must always have an adequate system of defence and a national sentiment in favour of such a system.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I never said anything like that.

The Address

Mr. Lawson

I beg pardon; I mean the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). The point I should like to make is this: At about the same time an editorial appeared in the Montreal Star suggesting that it might be in the best interests of all concerned if the government should withhold this information. Of course I do not know what action the government will take; but let me say this: I know that every war in the past has been called a war of defence. I know also when it is supposed to be in the interests of the people generally that certain information should be withheld, that has been done. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I for one will not permit one drop of Canadian blood to be shed until the. people of this country have been fully advised as to all the circumstances, and until they fully understand why they may be called upon to give up their lives.
That is about all I wish to say this evening. When the time comes, certain measures will have to be discussed, and I feel sure that then the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will certainly know we are an independent group. I am very glad the Prime Minister made that statement with regard to the independent groups. The first thing I was told when I came to the House of Commons was that I had to swear allegiance to a king. At first I did not know whether it was Mackenzie King or His Majesty the King, but I am glad the Prime Minister has cleared up that point for us. So I will now take my seat, assuring the right hon. gentleman of independent and fair co-operation and criticism when the time arrives.

Mr. Speaker, in view of some of the accusations levelled at my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) during the course of his remarks this afternoon, I feel it incumbent upon me to make some observations before this debate is concluded.
Before doing so, however, I would crave your indulgence to digress for a moment in order to congratulate the mover (Mr. Slaght) and the seconder (Mr. Fournier, Maisonneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and I trust that I shall not be considered invidious if I particularly congratulate one of my fellow practitioners of law from the city of Toronto on the eloquence, moderation and good taste of the speech he made in this house as his initial effort.
I had rather anticipated that the Prime Minister, banked about as he is at the present time by a vast majority which overflows from
your right, sir, to your left in this house, would have proceeded with all dispatch to bring into being those measures of legislation which during the campaign we were led to believe would bring a great era of unparalleled prosperity to Canada.

They are already
started.

I am glad to know that. I sincerely hope, in the interests of this country, that if an era of prosperity has started since my hon. friends came into power, it will continue. I for one, despite what was indicated by the Prime Minister in some of his utterances this afternoon, will be delighted to find this country enjoying prosperity, and I shall not try to decry any prosperity that we may attain simply because the Liberal party happens to be in power when it comes.
I said, sir, that I had anticipated that instead of the right hon. gentleman taking up the time of the house in criticism of the fact that some of the ministers of the former government had retired from public life and accepted office, something which has been done under governments with which .the right hon. gentleman has been associated in the past, he would have gone on with the business of bringing in this era of prosperity. It seems to me, sir, that it is rather small business to criticize the retirement and appointment of one whose name, I believe, was mentioned, Mr. Guthrie, who was almost the dean of this house, who had rendered at least thirty years of public service to this country, because he saw fit at a ripe age to retire and to accept an appointment. I oould say the same thing with reference to several of the other gentlemen who were named this afternoon or indicated by the right hon. Prime Minister. Though I am neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet, yet mark my words that before the next general election in this country some of the hon. gentlemen who now sit in the government led by the right hon. gentleman will be retiring and accepting some appointments which are in the gift of this country.
Some are already waiting.

Then the right hon. gentleman had some slighting references to make to the smallness of the number of Conservatives returned to this house in the last election. I confess, sir, that we are small in number. But I suggest to the right hon. gentleman that if he brings down legislation which in the opinion of this small number is not beneficial to Canada, if he brings down
The Address-Mr. Lawson

legislation which contravenes the principles of that great ipanty which I have the honour to support, he will soon find that the strength of our opposition is not limited by our numbers.
The right hon. gentleman attributed1-I was not quite sure whether it was his great success in the last election or cnur defeaL-in the main to three causes: one man government, all expenditures or commitments not approved by parliament before being made, and the organization of the Liberal party, which, he boasted, commenced on the first day after the defeat of that party in the 1930 election. Well, sir, with reference to one man government let me say this: I was not a member of the recent administration for a great length of time, but I want to make it clear that while I was, every matter of policy enunciated by the leader of this party was given every consideration, or opportunity for consideration, by the members who supported him in that government.
With respect to the expenditures under the blank cheque policy of which we have heard so much, it seems to me this is but reiteration and repetition time after time of something that in principle is very simple. This parliament has power to vote money and to make expenditures. Likewise this parliament has power to delegate that authority, under certain conditions and within the limits prescribed by parliament, to what I might term the executive of parliament, or what is known as the government. Now in our everyday lives we spend millions of dollars to provide hospitals for the care of our physical needs in case of emergency. During the past five years there were not many days when the government of this country did not have to face an emergency in connection with our economic life. And all this parliament did in granting power within the limits of the statute to the executive to expend money to meet economic situations which might arise to provide those emergency hospitals so necessary to meet such needs. Let us assume, for example, that it had been necessary for Canada to convene parliament when the United Kingdom went off the gold standard, before any action could be taken by the government of this country. Does my right hon. friend suggest that during the term the Conservative government were in power there were not emergencies, emergencies which had to be met not in six weeks or a month or two weeks but on the spur of the moment? Now, sir, this parliament, in anticipation of those emergencies which might arise in connection with our economic and financial and political system, delegated its power to

the executive, and that executive was just as responsible to parliament to give an accounting of its actions and its expenditures on the first occasion on which parliament convened as though the whole subject matter of the expenditure had been discussed in parliament before the expenditure was made.
The third reason that the right hon. gentleman gave was that the organization of the Liberal party commenced the day after the election in which they were defeated. With that I will entirely agree. It must have been obvious in the light of events during 1933 and 1934 that the Liberal party set up an organization after that election, and I give them credit for their sagacity in realizing as they did that the then Prime Minister of this country, the present right hon. leader of the oposition, was the outstanding figure in the government. So they determined that by their publicity they would "destroy Bennett," and by destroying Bennett they hoped to destroy the Conservative party. And I am quite willing to confess that, immersed in the affairs of state and the affairs of Canada, our great leader at times may have paid too little attention to the political fortunes of his party. Well, if it gives my hon. friends opposite any satisfaction I admit that the organization which they set up on the day subsequent to their defeat in 1930, and particularly their publicity, certainly did a good job for them.
Then the right hon. gentleman attributed to the leader of the opposition knowledge or responsibility for a poster appearing in western Canada. I say to you here and now, sir, that the leader of the official opposition never saw the poster-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Did you see it?
Yes, I saw it and I take the responsibility for it. What is more, the poster was true.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Why did you change it?

I did not change it. I was about to say that by the action taken by the Conservative government to protect and maintain the market for wheat for the wheat growers of western Canada, that government was responsible for putting into the pockets of the western grain growers at least $150,000,000. And when my hon. friends opposite see fit to bring down any legislation they may have with respect to the marketing of wheat or affecting the wheat board, I shall be glad, if necessary, to discuss the matter in further detail.

The Address-Mr. Lawson
The Prime Minister alleged that the leader of the opposition was responsible for the campaign literature of the Conservative party. If that be so, surely the same thing is equally true of the right hon. gentleman opposite; he too must be responsible for all the literature appearing on behalf of the Liberal party. Had I known that I was to participate in this debate, or could I have anticipated that the Prime Minister would have taken the line he did take, I should have been delighted to have before me, for the inspection of any hon. members who did not see them, some of the pamphlets turned out by the Liberal party during the last campaign.
May I mention one, which was a gem-from their standpoint. How many hon. members remember the consumer pamphlet?
The consumers' league?

No, not the consumers' league-and it was not the forgotten league, either. This was turned out under the auspices of the National Liberal Federation of Canada, and was directed particularly to Canadian housewives. On it appeared several pictures, one of which showed a can of baking powder. The text indicated how much a can of baking powder cost in Canada, and the cost in the United States. I think, too, there was a picture of a can of beans, and pictures of other household articles. The only thing that was prominently missing was a piece of buffalo bologna.
Was there a can opener?

No; my hon. friends
opposite felt that if they had supplied a can opener to Canadian housewives, the cans would have been opened and the emptiness, belied by the pictures, would have been discovered.
Like some people's heads.
Well, we will leave that to the judgment of posterity.
Thank 3'ou.

Down below the pictures there was the text to indicate that the higher prices for the commodities in Canada had been brought about by the Conservative government while in office between 1930 and 1935.
I say to you, sir, that I analyzed the tariffs indicated in the pamphlet, and if I had my papers with me this evening I could give you specific details. I am confident, however, that I am not overstating the misrepresentation contained in that pamphlet when I say to you that the tariffs in respect of over one-half the
articles pictured had been placed at their then rate by the government of the right hon. gentleman opposite when it held office previously, or by governments which preceded his accession to power.
If we want to get into the field of misrepresentation and responsibility for campaign literature, I could give my hon. friends one or two further examples. I have in mind another gem, and although I have forgotten the exact wording of it, the effect of it was this: "King will restore the markets Bennett and Stevens lost."
Bennett and Stevens what?
Bennett and Stevens lost."
So they did.

I will come to that in a
minute. If the right hon. gentleman is to take responsibility for the literature of his party, what do hon. members think of the fairness-and I use that word, for want of a better-of a gentleman who, for the purpose of a campaign couples with the present leader of the opposition the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens), and then after he has won the election endeavours in this House of Commons to twit the leader of the opposition by saying that this very member had turned his guns upon him, the leader of the opposition, during the campaign? Then, sir, I would ask this further question:	What market was lost to Canada
during the regime of the late Conservative government? Will some one tell me which one? Possibly someone will say Japan.

The market for salmon in
France.
Tell me one country.

The market for salmon in
France was lost.

Every tariff that was
raised against Canada had been raised before this party took office.
Oh, oh.

Let me refer to another
gem, "It is King or chaos."
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The old slogan.

The people decided
it.

I am not complaining
about the people's decision. Hon. members will never find me doing that. They may have observed that I happen to be one hon
The Address-Mr. Lawson

member in this chamber who sits in his seat and keeps his mouth shut, even when he has to take some punishment. I am not one who sits and cackles out once in a while, when someone else is speaking.
In other words the hon. member is not a rooster.

I really thought my good
friend, the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), with his breadth of experience and wisdom of age would know that a rooster never cackles.

Crows, then. I would not
like to call the hon. member an old hen.

This afternoon some
reference was made by the Prime Minister to a broadcast which he styled the Sage broadcast, and endeavoured again to place upon the leader of the opposition responsibility for it. I take this first opportunity to say to him and to this House of Commons that again I take the responsibility. We will see-
We saw.

I want to say this, that
in the rush and hurry and grind of a campaign some of the manuscripts were never submitted to me. So far as my recollection goes, there were put into the mouth of one of the speakers in those broadcasts two statements which, had I seen them, I would have deleted. I say unhesitatingly to the Prime Minister that I personally regret exceedingly that they were made, and for this reason:
I have always been, and I hope always shall be, one who in public life may criticize and assail my opponents with respect to their public actions and public affairs, but I do not believe I can be accused of ever having made a reference to their personal affairs or what they may have done in a personal capacity. Therefore I say that I regret two statements which were made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The references would have been all right if they had been true.
In justification for those who did use them, I just want to say this, that though you may not like the phrases, every statement made in the Sage broadcasts was true.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You will have a chance to prove that before a parliamentary committee.
Why do you regret them if they were true? You regretted them a moment ago.
Apparently my hon. friend from Antagonish-
Not Antagonish. I am not trying to antagonize anybody.
My hon. friend did not follow my statement.
Oh, yes, I did. I listened very carefully. You apologized first, and then you swallowed yourself.

I apologized for what I said was my recollection of two of the statements made because they referred to some action taken by the Prime Minister in his personal capacity, and not in his public capacity, and that is why I said I regretted exceedingly that they had been made.
I do not see the point.

Well, possibly not. Maybe my good friend is Scotch-I say this without intending any offence to that great race from which I come-and if he will go home and think the matter over the point may come to him by morning.
The trouble is that my hon. friend is not making any point. He starts apologizing, and then rubs it in and makes it worse.

The Prime Minister in speaking this afternoon expressed great concern for the well being of the employees of industry and of the workers and consumers in the community. When he gets on that theme he strikes a responsive chord because I happen to represent a lot of them in this house. I know it has been a favorite theme for the right hon. gentleman in both his writings and speeches since the days of his book, Industry and Humanity, if not prior to that, to exhibit in speech great concern for the workers in industry. But, sir, may I make the suggestion that at a recent date he had a wonderful opportunity to demonstrate in a very practical way his interest in the workers in industry in this country. It will be remembered by all that during the campaign the right hon. gentleman

The Address-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
went up and down this country telling us what a great day it would be if the Liberal party were returned to power in the Dominion of Canada because then, having Liberal governments in practically all the provinces of Canada, we would have one great happy family who would have no difficulty at all in agreeing. He repeated that sentiment to-day, if I recollect correctly, as to the happy associations of his government with those of the different provinces. It does seem to me that even though those of the Liberal party who were in the last house talked at great length against the constitutionality of the Unemployment and Social Insurance bill, and against the legislation respecting maximum hours of labour and minimum wages, I think ultimately, if they did not actually vote for those measures-and my recollection is that they did-at least they did not vote against them. Why? Because an election was coming, and they wanted to get the votes of the workers in this country. Well, when this happy family met, what a grand and glorious opportunity it would have been for the right hon. gentleman to say to the provincial premiers: Now, gentlemen, we are all Liberal friends; we are all members of the Liberal family; we have all a great desire to do something for the workers of this country; so just let us all agree that instead of referring these acts to the Supreme Court of Canada to determine the respective jurisdiction of dominion and province, we will all get together and have just one amendment to the British North America Act which will confer on the Dominion of Canada jurisdiction to pass these measures which are so very beneficial to the workers of this country.
In conclusion, sir, I say to you that when the right hon. gentleman demonstrates by some such action a practical interest in the workers of this country, I shall be much more prone to accept his policies and his preachings.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my hon. friend
who has just sat down (Mr. Lawson), I was quite willing to let the address be voted, but as he said that he intended to give the house some gems of the last election campaign, I cannot resist the temptation to imitate his example and not merely mention some of the gems but actually show them to the house.
Before doing so, Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer my congratulations to my good friend the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) and to the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemount (Mr. Fournier) for the excellent speeches which they delivered yesterday in moving and seconding the address
in reply to the speech from the throne. Both are valuable additions to the house and we are pleased to welcome them here.
My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) yesterday made some remarks which I might have left unanswered if they had come from a less important leader, but coming from him they cannot be considered as being what Disraeli described as the harebrained chatter of frivolous irresponsibility. I have to take account of my right hon. friend's statements, and so perhaps I may be permitted to mention two or three of them. I do not see why my right hon. friend was especially interested in making me the target of his attacks yesterday. But perhaps this is an honour. My right hon. friend has his likes and his dislikes, and it would appear now that I am rather classed with the latter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No? I
am glad to hear that. I thank my right hon. friend. However I can assure him that if he ascribes to me any large responsibility for the reverses which he may have had politically, he is wrong because I had very little share in the responsibility, and I want to assure him that whatever differences we . may have in politics I have nothing but the best of personal feelings towards him, feelings of respect and even admiration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are quite mutual.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The
right hon. gentleman spoke first of the election campaign in my province, and he mentioned certain words of mine. I am quite willing to admit that I have said that my province before 1930 had sent a very considerable, almost a solid Liberal following to the House of Commons, and that they had given a good account of themselves, and I certainly made an appeal to the electors of my province to do the same in 1935, because they realized that they had made a mistake in 1930. They agreed with me when polling day came. There was nothing very wrong in that.
My right hon. friend is quite wrong about the war cry, and I think he knows this. He will admit that he even used my words at two or three meetings in Quebec, in Montreal, in Sherbrooke, words which I had taken the trouble to write in order not to be misrepresented in the other provinces, as was the case in former elections. I took the trouble to say that I was sure that the leader of the opposition shared my views as to trying to keep
122	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Ixipointe (Quebec East)
Canada out of any conflict if it were at all possible, so that even my words were repeated by the right hon. gentleman in that respect.
The little paper which he quoted yesterday, and which seemed to be published in English, could not have had a very great effect upon the people of the province of Quebec. What was said in that paper? There was a dispatch from Ottawa to the effect that Canada could mobilize a powerful and fully experienced army within twenty-four hours, and the statement is made:
Canada will probably be drawn into the European war if Great Britain is forced in, and irrespective of what politicians, statesmen and economists say, the dominion will not be able to help herself.
I do not see anything there against the Conservative party or in favour of the Liberal party, but I have something which is quite different. Here is a paper which was circulated from door to door in my own city of Quebec in the last days of the election. It is entitled:
Ouvriers et Cultivateurs pensez-y bien! Protegez-vous. Workingmen and farmers, think well about it! Protect yourselves.
I will not mention all' the things that are said about Mr. Taschereaiu and the trusts and matters of that sort, but the last part of it reads:
Do not take a chance, and vote for Bennett. In case of war, who will protect your interests better? Do you know that Bennett has stated, "In case of a foreign war, not one cent, not one man, not one gun," while King contented himself with saying, "We will summon parliament and will decide afterwards." Do you know that Mr. Bennett was the irreconcilable opponent of conscription and that he has challenged the legality of it, as far as before the Supreme Court of Canada, while not a single Liberal member voted against the principle of that bill? In case of war who will protect your interests better? Do not take a chance, and vote for Bennett.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Apparently they did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wonder whether my good friend who has just spoken takes the responsibility for this.

I may advise my hon.
friend that anything for which I take the responsibility was turned out-and it will be marked plainly and distinctly upon it-either by the Confederation Publishing Company Limited or by the dominion Conservative headquarters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend will take the responsibility for some others.
I may, when I hear them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The war issue was only a very small one in the campaign. In my own province my leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) and I were described as the friends of the men who want to pull down the steeples, the men who protect those who walk on crucifixes, and so on. These things were published not only in leaflets distributed ; they appeared in paid advertisements in the newspapers of the province, bearing the inscription at the foot, "Published by the central Conservative committee."

That was not published
by the Conservative dominion headquarters, nor have we any knowledge of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, the Conservative branch in Quebec apparently enjoys its autonomy.
In that respect it is characteristic of all Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have their autonomy and they seem to have their money too. Apart from this terrible thing there were many others. Let me show this picture of a terrible looking man.
Enemy No. 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am mentioned as having stated my belief that when truth and error are being given a fair show to justify themselves, truth always prevails. That was described as a heresy, and the last words of course were, "Let us vote for Bennett," and "Published by the central Conservative committee," but that was a lie. Here is another one with a fine portrait of my right hon. friend:
Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, Prime Minister of Canada. Protect our Canadian country against communism.
Then there is some terrible picture, and it concludes with these words:
Vote for Bennett, the only political leader who upholds the maintenance of section 98, the only leader of a state who understands the horrible threat which is on our country, the only leader able to protect the nation. A vote for Bennett is a vote for your home. A vote for Bennett is a vote for the respect of right, of religion, of tradition. Published by the central Conservative committee.
Well, that is the sort of campaign we had, and the radio was also used to spread this propaganda. On the Sunday, the eve of polling day, the radio was used in my own constituency to describe me as a terrible man, an enemy of all religion and virtue and everything, and it was stated that if the Prime Minister and I were returned to power the poor children would be forced to go to church

The Address-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
and commit deeds of sacrilege, and that sort of stuff. Of course, the effect was that on the following day, instead of having a majority of 2,000, which was the usual one, I was elected by a majority of 6,000.
1 wish to go very quickly over two or three matters relating to the proposed sanctions on oil. a subject which was very well explained by my right hon. leader this afternoon. I have been very much abused for having stated what was, after all, the truth with regard to the position of Canada. It was not properly a repudiation of any man; it was the repudiation of what was being stated everywhere in the world, that it was Canada that was proposing this oil sanction, when so many countries were disquieted and did not know what to do about it. We merely said that we had not given any instructions to that effect; that this was not a Canadian proposal; that Canada was quite willing to have the same responsibility as the other countries, to join in any collective action to try to secure the maintenance of peace, but that we had not gone out of our way to attempt to force the other nations of the world to apply this oil sanction against Italy. This has been misrepresented in many places, and, I must say, more particularly in the very good city of Toronto.
I hesitate to do this, but I desire to show another gem, a cartoon against which I wish to register a strong protest. The Evening Telegram, which is a newspaper very distinguished along certain lines, attacked me very bitterly about this question, as regards which I had done merely what I thought to be my duty, what I thought to be right. I did not mind the blame in the editorials; but when it came to this cartoon which I hold in my hand, entitled " His Master's Voice," where I am seen pulling the coat of Doctor Riddell at the League of Nations, and there is a priest in clerical garb, with a biretta, whispering in my ears, with the inscription " His Master's Voice," well, I think, after being thirty-two years in the public service of my country, if I had no right to take a stand on a public matter and to say to the people of Canada what I think is right, because I am French and Roman Catholic, we have not achieved in Canada the progress which we thought we had achieved, .and there is certainly room for reform. However, things like that do not affect a man in such a way as to induce him to quit the service of his country. I am not a quitter; I always face those who attack me. But I did not mind so much even the campaign of the Toronto Telegram as the words I read in an article well written, broadly conceived, written by a gentleman for whom
I have great respect, a fine Canadian, Professor Norman Mackenzie of the university of Toronto, an editorial in Saturday Night of December 21, entitled "Confusion in Canadian Foreign Policy." The article is impartially written, praising and blaming; but here are the words which show the necessity of the remarks I 'have just offered with regard to the Toronto Telegram. Professor Mackenzie says:
While this statement may have been necessary, it has had most unfortunate results, both in Canada and internationally. Obviously, as a French Roman Catholic, Mr. Lapointe was the last one who should have made it, for it was immediately seized upon by the opposition as a repudiation of Great Britain ...
And so forth. Of course this does not represent, I know, the views of Professor Mackenzie ; but as he told me afterwards, it represents the views of many people whom he meets almost daily in his own city. I have said enough on this subject. I hope that this question as well as any other public question in Canada can be treated on its merits, without anybody going down to the level of dealing with it on religious and racial grounds, as is done in this cartoon.
As to the references to the supreme court, I do not apologize for having made a recommendation to the government to that effect. My right hon. friend says that even if some of these acts were doubtful, or may be unlawful, the government should have waited until somebody took action before the courts to have them declared invalid. I do not agree with this method of proceeding. Possibly some of them would not involve very great financial commitments, but on some of these measures the people of Canada, employers and employees and governments, would have incurred heavy expenses even from the beginning. It is better to have the validity and the legality of these measures passed upon before incurring expenses than after they have been incurred.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will it disturb the hon. gentleman if I point out to him that he has not grasped the point I was endeavouring to make? I stated the privy council had said that an opinion expressed by the supreme court would be no better than that of the law officers of the crown, and therefore there was no finality to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Except that an opinion of the supreme court, and possibly of the privy council, because there is an appeal to the privy council in these matters, certainly would carry great moral weight with the people of Canada and with the interested parties. May I refresh the
124	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
memory of my right hon. friend by reminding him that even his government resorted to this procedure of making references to the supreme court? The year preceding the enactment of this legislation the government referred to the Supreme Court of Canada the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act. There was a second reference under section 110 of the Dominion Companies Act, and there was a reference on the tariff board. Apparently my right hon. friend and his colleagues thought a legal opinion given by the Supreme Court of Canada was of some value, and they obtained that opinion before enforcing the measures upon the validity of which they desired the opinion of that body. As my right hon. friend has said, we appointed th'e best available counsel to present the views of the dominion in the matter. I admit that I expressed contrary views on the floor of the house last year, but if my right hon. friend will remember, I told him at the time that I was not as sure of my views as he was of his; that I would be very happy if I could be. At that time both my right hon. leader and I suggested that these acts should be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada; we asked that they should be, and we stated definitely that we would have them referred if we were members of the future government of the country.
Then my right hon. friend mentioned the commission which is investigating the unfortunate troubles which took place in Regina last spring. I must remind him that that is a provincial commission which was appointed by the government of Saskatchewan before the last general election.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It did not begin to
function until after the election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is true. The then Minister of Justice took the view that the province had no right to appoint these judges as commissioners; that the dominion should appoint them from Ottawa, and the commission was notified accordingly. Chief Justice Brown of Saskatchewan, Mr. Justice Martin of the appeal court and Judge Doak, the three commissioners, said that they would be only too pleased not to be compelled to serve on that commission, but that they could not see their duties as they were seen by the then Minister of Justice; they thought they were compelled to act. They offered their resignations to the provincial government and asked to be relieved from serving on the commission, but the provincial government refused to accept their resignations and stated 
that it had the right to appoint it. That was the situation when I took charge of the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But no judge has a duty to act. He is not bound to act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was the position taken by Chief Justice Brown in the letters he wrote, which form part of the record. However I must say that my views in that respect differ from those of my predecessor. I had occasion to consider this matter in some instances prior to 1930. I had the legal opinion of the late Mr. Justice Newcombe, then deputy minister of Justice, who advised me at the time that judges could act on those provincial commissions. I merely followed the precedent which was created at that time and which was followed even by my predecessor in the department until this incident occurred in Regina.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Oh, no. The province of Ontario, for a long time, requested that the dominion should agree to the appointment of judges for these purposes; then it ceased to do so. Whatever it may mean, the statute says that the consent of the dominion should be sought and given. Mr. Justice Neweombe's view was that this did not have reference to a provincial commission. I recall the circumstances, but the difficulty is tJhat judges cease to be judges the moment they accept a commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But they are commissioners acting at the request of the province and performing a public service. Of course the only knowledge I have of the matter is from the records, but I must tell my right hon. friend that in connection with the hydro commission inquiry in Ontario the _ minister admitted that this action was taken by the province alone without authorization from Ottawa, though he stated that this did not alter the fact that the authorization should come from Ottawa.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
However, that is a matter as to which we must be permitted to differ. This commission is going on; its work is proceeding, I think, in a most effective way. I do not think there were any politics in its appointment. This is merely a means of getting at the truth of a matter which was debated between the provincial and the federal governments. What made it perhaps still more imperative that this should be done was the fact that Saskatchewan is policed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who receive their orders in provincial matters

The Address-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
from t.he attorney general of the province and in federal matters, of course, from Ottawa. There was a conflict between the two authorities, and I sincerely believe that the work of the commission and its report, instead of intensifying this friction and conflict, may make it easier to reconcile the two views. My right hon. friend stated that the morale of the police has declined because of the appointment of this commission. Far from it. I believe the evidence that is being given before the commission will rather be a justification of what the police did, and will rather clarify certain issues which were perhaps dangerous, as to which the people did not have the best information, the information they should have had.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was dealing with the effect upon the trial of the accused.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think so. My right hon. friend referred to the fact that the chief justice permitted one of the strikers to say that the victim of the battle had been killed by one of the mounted police officers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That he saw the officer battering the man to death.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. How could the chief justice refuse to hear that man? That is what that witness said, but there were scores of witnesses, both police and neutral citizens, who said otherwise. After all, the only way to get at the truth is to secure the evidence of all those who claim to have been witnesses to what took place at that time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I agree, only the matter should be in a court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It should be in a court, but it is difficult to get a matter like that into a court.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But it is in a court now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It could be in court only in connection with one special incident having to do with the accused on trial in that court. Now my right hon. friend said it is even stated that evidence would be taken in British Columbia. Possibly one of the commissioners is going there. But it is to serve the ends of justice and it may happen that the evidence given there might be far from injurious to the case of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was not concerned about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is exactly as I said already, to get the facts. Surely it is not a bad thing to get the facts and to find where the truth is, no more in this matter than in the reference to the supreme court, and even in the Riddell incident. Those strikers, or a committee representing them, came to see me since the commencement of this investigation. They asked three things: first, that we should appoint a dominion commission instead of that provincial commission which apparently they do not like; second, that we should change the personnel of the commission, increase it and put a representative of the strikers on it. Of course we could not very well agree to that. Their third request was that we should pay counsel for the strikers. Those three demands were submitted to me and to some of my colleagues, and after consideration we rejected them. We thought the present commission has all the necessary powers to secure what we want to have shown, and the facts. We did not give them what they desired, but they paid us the compliment of saying it was the first time for years that they had been received courteously when they came to Ottawa.
Now there is another matter which also relates to the administration of justice. I am prevented from referring to it except, without giving any names, to say that far from being actuated by politics in this matter, certain people had made the same demand before 1930. There had been a subsequent trial of another man, who had been acquitted in connection with the same matter, and the man who had been convicted claimed that this made a change and that there had been a mistrial. The attorney general of Ontario advised strongly against a new trial. I refused to recommend a new trial before 1930. Surely this was not because of politics, for the attorney general of Ontario then was a Conservative. But when I came back to the department this year there had been an investigation held by the present attorney general of Ontario, who had made a new report strongly recommending the granting of a new trial. This report had been submitted to my immediate predecessor in office, who was there only a short time, but he did not deal with it; he had no time, and I found it on the doorstep. Conditions were altogether changed. But, Mr. Speaker, even then I did not feel like granting a new trial. I thought the ends of justice would be better served by using the discretionary power which I have under the criminal code to refer the whole matter to the court of appeal of Ontario, and to let them decide what should be done. I thought, in
The Address-Mr. Douglas

face of the conflict between the two attorney's general of Ontario, the one prior to 1930 and the one of to-day, the best thing for the Department of Justice here to do was to refer the question for judicial determination in the province, and I do not think I deserve to be told by my right hon. friend that some people are afraid there are politics in the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I did not say politics. Look and see what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, I hope it is not that, because if my right hon. friend said it he knows the gravity and the seriousness of such a remark.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I fully realize it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: However, I think I may close these remarks by telling my right hon. friend that I hope he will think well of me in the future as he did in the past. As far as I am concerned I wish him happiness and peace. My best and most earnest wish is that he may be brought to feel kindly about his political opponents.

Mr. Speaker, first I wish to take this opportunity of congratulating you upon your accession to the position which you now hold. I wish also to congratulate the mover (Mr. Slaght) and the seconder (Mr. Fournier) of the address.
In rising to speak to this motion I feel that not only do I represent the constituency of Weyburn; that not only do I represent a group in this house which holds a particular social viewpoint, but that as one of the youngest members in this house I represent a class of people in Canada who hitherto have been unrepresented. Might I point out that there are perhaps more young men in this House of Commons than there have been for many years past. I feel we can say, because of the contacts which some of us have with youth organizations across the dominion, that through us to some extent a certain section of young Canada speaks.
I wish to draw the attention of the house to one remarkable phrase in the speech from the throne, a phrase which seems to me to be pregnant with irony. It is this:
-in adhering to the aims and ideals of the League of Nations, and in seeking, in unison with members of the league as well as with other nations, to support by all appropriate and practical means the maintenance of peace, and the establishment of a world order based on justice and equity.
I should like this house to think for a moment of what that means and what steps the government has taken to maintain peace.
[Mr. E. Lapomte.i
I need hardly remind hon. members that in 1919 at the close of the great war the League of Nations was formed, and that in signing the covenant of the league, for the first time in the history of the human race over fifty nations gave up their sovereign right to wage war. But in return for giving up that right these fifty-seven nations required that they in turn would be guaranteed collective security. That after all is the only way that you and I can ever hope to live in a law-abiding and peaceful world. Just as you and I within the state, by giving up certain privileges of attacking the person of another individual, receive certain protection and certain privileges, so the nations of the world began this noble experiment of giving up the sovereign right to wage war and in return were guaranteed collective security.
Following that, Italy is declared by the nations of the league to be an aggressor against Ethiopia. I want here and now to commend the present administration upon two things which they have done. They interpreted correctly the mind of the Canadian people, first when they decided that the people wanted economic sanctions, and, second, when they correctly decided that the Canadian people did not want to indulge in a world war. That is, they understand what I suggest is the basic psychology of the Canadian people to-day, namely, that we will not trade with a murderer while he is engaged in the act of murdering, and that we will not have any trade or traffic with any brigand while he is engaged in international piracy. That I believe to be the attitude of the Canadian people, and the government correctly interpreted it.
What happened? We went through the motions of passing economic sanctions-and I say "through the motions," because it is very evident that sanctions have only one aim and one purpose, namely, to prevent war. Sanctions are valuable only if they are made effective. For instance we know today that it is absolute nonsense to talk about passing sanctions against Italy or any other country if the sanctions which are passed have the effect of boycotting commodities which are not needed by that country for purposes of war. Italy can get along without Christmas trees, Christmas candles and teddy bears, but there are certain basic commodities without which she cannot wage a war.
I believe Doctor Riddell took the logical position that if sanctions are to be valuable they must be effective, and that the most effective sanction in this day and age would be oil. Napoleon said that an army marches on its stomach; the modem army marches

The Address-Mr. Douglas
on oil. Without oil Italy could not continue to fight. What happened? The Canadian government gave the impression throughout the civilized world that Canada was not prepared to stand behind the statement that had been made by her representative. This afternoon the Prime Minister explained that what was meant was something similar to the statement made by Sir Samuel Hoare. That however was not the interpretation placed upon it, and I believe the statement was open to the interpretation that Canada was not in favour of oil sanctions.
There are two sources from which Italy has been drawing her oil, namely, the Anglo-Persian Oil Company of Great Britain and the Standard Oil Company of the United States. When Mr. Lloyd George made the statement during the last general election campaign in Great Britain that aeroplanes flying over Ethiopia had Anglo-Persian oil in their petrol tanks, the reply of the president of that company was significant. He said, "We are keeping the sanction; we are making Italy pay cash." In other words the only crime that, in the minds of certain financial interests could be perpetrated would be that of giving credit to Mussolini. Because of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company in Great Britain and the influence that had been brought to bear in this country, we find today that oil sanctions are much further away than when they were first suggested. Why is that so? Is it because the oil interests have too much influence on the powers of government? Is it because those people who make their profits out of oil have a great deal more weight in the councils of the governments of the world than have the dictates of humanity?
The speech from the throne speaks about maintaining peace-peace to-day, when Canadian nickel is indirectly being shipped to Ethiopia. Peace to-day, when Italian aeroplanes are being flown with British oil! Peace! Mr. Speaker, if this be peace it must be like the peace of the Lord-it passeth all understanding. Hon. members in this comer of the chamber voice a logical protest. If the government is going to talk about sanctions, we urge that they be effective sanctions. The people of Canada are asking that we take a definite stand in the matter, a stand with the forces of peace rather than with those of financial interests desiring a greater sale of oil.
I would point out that the speech from the throne is notable not so much for what it says as for what it fails to say.
That is a good one.

If it ever becomes famous it will do so because it is the speech that forgot the forgotten man. I come from a part of Canada that knows something of destitution and poverty. Last winter the church of which I was minister distributed large quantities of clothing contributed by people in Ontario, part of which came from this city of Ottawa. Tons of clothing were distributed throughout the southern area. I am sure hon. members will realize that I am not drawing on my imagination when I state that last fall there were children going to school in Saskatchewan with only gunny sacking wrapped around their feet. We have gone into homes and found mothers and children lying on piles of bedding in the corner; they did not have the proper bedding equipment or the proper clothing to meet the rigours of a very cold winter. In those sections where necessity for food, clothing and shelter is dire and where people are faced with want and insecurity, what do we find? We find that in this entire speech there is hardly a reference to what is to be done for them. What has the government of the day to offer to these people harassed with debt, needing food and needing clothing?
I hold in my hand a letter from my constituency, one of hundreds which are received by members. This is one from Trossachs, Saskatchewan. I shall not weary hon. members by reading it all, but I would direct their attention to some words from this man whom I have known, a man who has worked for years to help build the province of Saskatchewan and the Dominion of Canada. Men like these are the assets of our country. He states:
I have been trying to get relief. They allowed me $1.35 a month to live on, and would not allow me anything for clothes, and that is something that I really need. But I do not want to get anything I do not need, but I sure need clothes.
He wants only enough clothing to keep warm. I now hold in my hand a letter from one of my committee men. It is addressed from Montmartre, Saskatchewan, at which point he investigated a case, one which is by no means isolated. It could be duplicated again and again. The letter is as follows:
There is a family of eleven persons here living on relief. They are getting eight dollars per month, and range in age from thirteen to twenty-six. This family is starving. Two of them are under the doctor's care through not having enough to eat. Will you please see what you can do for this family? I am helping them all I can at present, hut that is not very much. I know families in this district that are getting more than eight dollars a month, with only three in the family. So
The Address-Mr. Douglas

would you please let me know what can be done for this family? I have just come from a visit there, and they had dry bread and
potatoes for supper.
This may seem a very trivial matter to an august assembly such as this, but I want to tell you, sir, that watching the house this night are families all over the dominion who are facing conditions like that, men, women and children who are looking to this new administration, with its preponderant majority, to bring them some measure of relief from their present hardships. As the hour is getting late I shall defer what further remarks I have to make until to-morrow.
On motion of Mr. Douglas the debate was adjourned.

stagedirection
speechtext: Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec East) moved the adjournment of the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Before the motion is put, I would point out that the government notice of motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister with respect to the trade agreement does not set out the agreement itself. It will be recalled that last year when we were dealing with matters of that kind we thought it desirable to put the agreement or convention or whatever it might be on the orders of the day, so that members of the house would have it before them when they came to approve the agreement. We printed for the convenience of the members the various conventions that had been signed at Geneva in order that they might have it before them when ratification or approval was moved. I suggest therefore that the trade agreement should be set out on the orders of the day so that it will be available to the members for we must insist on having before us the agreement before we approve it in some form or another.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, my right hon. friend knows that the agreement, and especially the schedules, is a very voluminous document, and if it were put on the orders of the day and stood there for days, because it is not going to be taken up immediately, it would increase the size of the order paper. Perhaps it might be printed in a separate document, or in the votes and proceedings for one day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will consult the Prime Minister about the matter.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
[Mr Douglas.]
